subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS ON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday. December 5, consideration in committee of bill No. 15, to confer certain powers upon the governor in council during the national emergency following the war-Mr. St. Laurent- Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 2-Continuation of national emergency.	,

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS ON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Last night I was referring to section 2 of the bill, which confers certain powers upon the governor in council. I pointed out that these powers are greater than the governor in council had in time of war. One of the paragraphs refers to assisting the relief of suffering, the restoration and distribution of essential supplies, and so forth. For many years past I have objected to these controls and the people who are in charge of them. Some of those controllers have no knowledge of the business they seek to control; they have never had any training in any competitive business.
In Australia the control system has been abolished. In the United States President Truman has said that controls placed upon the

National Emergency
country in time of war should be removed. Irksome controls which make it utterly impossible for a small man to conduct his business should be removed. A great many men are returning from the war and are trying to set up little shops where they can conduct their business, but they are unable to do it.
The original bill not only gives the minister the powers of the War Measures Act but has added a whole lot of controls nobody ever heard of, virtually abolishing the high court of parliament. Under this new bill whole spheres of activity, involving the livelihood of every man, woman and child in this country, have been removed from the jurisdiction of the law and of parliament and reserved for the determination of tribunals, irresponsible, irremovable, governed by no control and subject to no appeal. I object to that. It is done over the head of parliament, although they say parliament is supreme. That is only a myth; every business man knows it is a myth, with the result that parliamentary institutions are criticized by the people to-day, since we are to blame for the appointment of all these controllers.
I was saying something about a young soldier who came home and wanted to get a store. He went to a real estate man in my constituency and applied for one. The real estate man said:	'T cannot do anything for
you." The soldier said:	"I can finance a
little store right now"; but because of those irksome controls over business and real estate he was not permitted to start that little business. I do not know who wants to own real estate to-day.
I visited Cleveland and other cities a short time ago and I found that they are removing and relaxing those controls with the result that large and small businesses are expanding, not only in real estate, but in building and everything else. The other day they abolished meat rationing, if you please. We have been hanging on to the coat-tails of Washington all the time. One of the greatest mistakes we made in this war was the surrendering of too [DOT]much political, economic, social, financial and military initiative to Washington, with the result that we are simply hanging on to the coat-tails of the United States to develop our economic system. You go to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and the Minister of Labour, and what do you get?
I wish to refer to the section dealing with assisting the relief of suffering. One of the local newspapers, the Journal, had a long editorial yesterday on what is being done to get domestic and nursing help. In the session of the spring of 1944 I referred to what has been done in the old' country. Go to any hospital,
and you cannot get a nurse. Go to any large hotel and ask for a nurse. Can you get one? No. I know some of the large hotels have them on duty twenty-four hours a day, but in the average city throughout Canada you cannot get nursing service if you happen to be sick while at a hotel.
I asked a question in the house about the scarcity of domestic help and nurses, and here is the return that was brought down. Go and ask any business man who is connected with a hospital about the difficulty of getting nurses; go and ask any person who wants domestic help. They cannot get them, and they blame these controls. Go around the country and see the great number of people travelling on the trains and crowding the stations, and you will see why we can get no relief. In Britain, the United States, New Zealand and Australia they have adopted policies to provide domestic help and nurses, but we have done nothing in this country. Take the awful horror of the motor car; this year 85 people were killed in automobile accidents in the city in which I live. Take the number of accidents on the highway, and you will find that the number of people killed and injured in automobile accidents during the war almost equalled the number lost in the war itself. When those who suffer these accidents are taken to hospitals where there is a shortage of nurses, it is a burden oq the hospital. When I ask questions on these matters in this house, what is done? Ask any business man who is to blame for these conditions, and he will tell you. We have a large number of people still in the armed forces who should have been released long ago. Under this particular clause I cannot refer to the Department of Labour, but I can mention these matters under this paragraph dealing with the relief of suffering. They are spending $13,000,000 on national selective service, a system that might as well be dumped in the sewer. The minister is not here, and I do not wish to be unfair to him, but that is one of the reasons there is no domestic help available.
I asked a short question, covering only three lines, as to what was being done by the government to provide domestic help and nursing services for those with large families and for the sick. In England they have remedied that situation. Part of the reply came from the Department of Health and Welfare, the health part of which is only a skeleton branch because the municipalities and the provinces pay for health. What do they say about the lack of nurses?
National Emergency

The proposals by the government of Canada placed before the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction-
Castles in the air!
-would provide financial assistance to provinces which adopt health insurance to provide visiting nurse service and other services for all persons qualified	
Then with regard to domestic health:
The offices of the national employment service throughout the country are making every effort to meet the demand for domestic workers.
I should mention the list of telephones that selective service has in the city of Toronto. One morning I wasted nearly forty-five minutes calling about eight different numbers, and I could not get anybody who knew anything about what I wanted. They would simply hang up the receiver. That is the kind of service we are getting there, and it might just as well be closed up. The member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) is chairman of the splendid East Toronto hospital board, a man who has worked hard for my city in many capacities, and I cannot speak too highly of his services. He knows of this scarcity. No hospital board can put up with this sort of thing any longer. You cannot get a room in a hospital; you cannot get a nurse; you cannot get domestic help. What is the reason? It is national selective service, and keeping people in the forces.
Let me point out to the committee the reason for that. I am speaking extemporaneously and without notes, but I can give you one reason. Most of these people travelling on the trains are members of the armed forces and their families. As the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Poulioty said the other day, speaking of Sparks street, you cannot go out into the highways and by-ways; you have to stay in the middle of the road because so many of the armed forces are kept there who want to return to business. Let us do what they are doing in the mother country; let us try to get rid of some of these irksome controls. I will admit that some controls are necessary to guard against inflation, high prices for food and all that sort of thing, and I will admit that the Minister of Finance has done very excellent work in that connection. The controls required to regulate the prices of the necessaries of life should be continued; but the controls essential during the war, when the majority of the orders in council were passed, were dictated by the needs of the state. In peace time, as a Conservative committee in England said, the preference of consumers is the mainspring of economic activity. Although controls will be essential

during a transitional period for organizing the reversion from war to peace time conditions they must be .removed as soon as conditions permit. That is Mr. Churchill's policy, and the policy of his party; and the committee goes on to say that since controls have no intrinsic value in themselves they are liable to lead to hold-ups and thereby slow down the speed of industry to adjust itself to consumers' needs. That committee went on to make these specific recommendations:
(1)	Controls will be required in the immediate post-war period for the orderly disposal of accumulated stocks throughout the world, whether of foodstuffs or materials; for helping to right the adverse balance of payments and for dealing with shortages, but not otherwise.
(2)	A practical measure of control over the location of new industrial undertakings in Britain is desirable as a permanent feature of the post-war world. It may thus be possible to secure a balance of different types of industry in each main region of the country, thereby lessening the risks of severe unemployment in any one area.
(3)	A continuous survey must be carried on by a properly qualified national advisory body with local assistance, which will draw the attention of parliament to the emergence of dangerous features in the industrial situation of any particular area, and will formulate proposals for remedying them.
So you see they are trying to do something over there. In Britain the government proposed a term of five years, while the Conservative opposition suggested two years. In this country it should be no longer than six months; it should be well over by Easter at the very latest. In the early days of this war, when controls were being established, I asked the Minister of Finance a question as to whether he sees the orders issued by the control boards, in reply to which he made a lengthy statement in the house. I asked if he ever saw these piles of orders in council issued about food, clothing and all these other things. I believe his reply was no, that a general direction of policy was given and that was all he had to do with it.
By passing clause 2 we are paving the way for the return of the conditions we had previously. I blame the government because they are afraid to release those who should be released under the national service act, so these irksome controls may be abolished. It is either inefficiency on the part of the government or it is fear of turning these people out because of the effect it may have on the labour market. The government of the day should have far more courage than they have shown so far in seeking to relieve the conditions from which we are suffering, by returning to industry larger numbers of men and women. Now real estate is going to be

National Emergency
controlled for two years under this measure. No one will want to own real estate. The hon. member for Eglinton, is not here, but it will be remembered that some days ago he spoke about housing. People in his riding cannot hold their real estate and use their property. Soldiers who are buying properties cannot move into them, owing to irksome controls on real estate, with the result that they find themselves out on the streets, with the bailiffs after them. Others are under eviction orders and have nowhere to go.
I would ask the government to look at the picture as we find it throughout the country in the cities and towns. There is not a neighbourhood in Canada where families .are not having difficulty in connection with housing, and if this bill is passed they will be tied up for one or two more years. In all our cities and towns men and women wish to end all the confusion and get back to their homes so that they can enter into small business enterprises.
I say this bill is much worse than the old one, because in it there is no control whatsoever which can be exercised by the courts. I pointed out on September 11 that any order in council can be revoked by the high court of parliament, through the process of some hon. member moving in the house that such order in council be annulled. But that is not so under the War Measures Act.
In my opinion the left was never right, either in war or in peace. We know that those belonging to the left went up and down this country, saying that we could depend upon collective security and league pacts without defences and armies, and all that sort of thing. But what happened when war came along? What was the result? We had no army, no navy or air force. Our navy was scarcely any size-less than a total of
10,000	tons. I do not say this in an*' spirit of disrespect for those who sit to my left, because they are pleasant gentleman, always courteous in debate, and I wish to show them the same courtesy, as we cannot all think alike on public matters. I must say however that I believe they are and were wrong. Everyone is entitled to his opinion, and that is mine. Some go-around the country posing as supermen, and it was they who supported pacifism in the past. If this section is passed, then that will just about finish everything.
Since the beginning of this session we have heard a lot from the left about internationalism and almost nothing about the empire. Well, we know what it did for us in two great wars in our generation, and we think we can see what it will do for us now in this time of reconstruction. Let us wait and see what will be
done by collective security and a new league. It will mean the dissolution of the British empire which saved the world in this war.
Paragraph (a) of this section provides for the maintenance of the armed forces, and all that sort of thing. I can tell you this, that there is only one way to solve this question, and that is for the dominions and the mother country to hold together. If we do not hold together historically, geographically, economically and from a military standpoint, we will not be able to go it alone and we will hang separately. We must, as an empire, hold together if we are not to perish. In Britain they have always been our best customers, and in the dark days they were our only friends. But it would seem now that we are willing to toss them overboard, through certain international agreements which can be made under order in council. I protest against that sort of procedure, as I have protested against it many times in the past. I continue to do so.
The plan set out in this bill is the Donald Gordon plan, and the plan to which the dominion-provincial conference objected. If that is the plan, then it is one which will have the effect of abolishing the high court of parliament. In my opinion Donald Gordon should have been dismissed long ago and irksome controls removed.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS ON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr.	Chairman, I
return to section 2, subsection 3, with which must be read-if you will allow me-section 4. Both are part and parcel of the same transaction. As has been stated before, new regulations which will be passed under this measure as now constituted will be laid on the table of the house; but the great mass of orders in council that have been passed during the war under the War Measures Act will be incorporated into the law of the land, Regardless of their nature, their interference with the rights of justice, or their unfairness, parliament will be approving those orders in council and will have no opportunity of annulling them, as it will in respect of new orders in council passed after this date.
I am not going to discuss again the situation respecting these orders in council. The minister explained last night that they were in six volumes.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; I think there are eight volumes of orders and proclamations, and there must be a larger number of war orders and regulations.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS ON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I appreciate that. But there were six large volumes, and then every few weeks a further assortment of orders comes out and is published in these periodicals.

National Emergency
The minister showed what they had in Great Britain, and, producing the volume, he said: This is,.the volume of the orders in council passed in Great Britain. Compare this with the depth of the volumes passed by this government, and you have some appreciation of the far more extensive use of orders in council by this'country.
Among the orders in council to which objection has been taken during the period of the war, which we have been unable to annul or amend, and concerning which we could do nothing but take objection, there are some which, although possibly justifiable during the war, deny recourse to the courts on the part of anyone who feels himself unfairly dealt with or discriminated against. There are orders in council which amend and abrogate statutes passed by parliament. These, if this measure is passed, now become the law of the land. Why should not parliament have the right to amend, abrogate, suspend or annul such orders in council as have been passed during the period of the war, and which from this day forward will become part and parcel of the legislation of the country?
I cannot see why the government is so resentful, if I may use that expression-and I believe I am justified in doing so, because of the speech made last night by the Minister of Justice-of any suggestion that parliament should have the right to annul such orders in council. Is it because it is realized that if they are looked into, unfairness will be brought to light? Is it because injustices would be revealed? There is not an hon. member who has not received strong objections respecting unfairness in connection with some of these orders. Is it because the government is afraid that the whole situation would be brought into parliament? If not, then why the objection to incorporating into this measure the right of parliament to annul orders in council passed during the war? What of the secret orders in council that we are going to pass under this section? How many are there? We got the answer some months ago that there were none, and then out came one with regard to Eldorado and then another concerning seamen's regulations. That was an order in council that denied recourse to the courts, denied a man the right to have counsel; and now we are asked to give a blank cheque -an expression to which the minister objects to the governor in council to deny to the individual seeking justice in this land the right to be represented by counsel. Its secrecy cannot be explained on the ground that there was need for secrecy in connection with the production of atomic energy, because this order had to do with seamen's regulations.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
This is one type of regulation we are asked to incorporate as part of the law of the land under section 4. The minister says: We will not use these powers; we just want them, that is all. What do they want them for if they are not going to use them? There is an important principle at stake here, and I cannot understand the resistance of the government to allowing parliament the right to look into these things. I am asking the minister whether even now he will accept a further amendment of this section. He says he gives an undertaking that if any hon. member wishes to attack any of these orders in council, either those that are being moved forward under the provisions of the War Measures Act or those that will be passed hereafter, the government will give assistance, his voice being heard in the house. I accept that statement, but I ask: Why not, so far as those old orders in council go, give us our rights under statute so that the people of this country will know, not only that we have an undertaking but that we have the right within a period of fifteen days after the beginning of the next parliament to demand the rescinding of unfair orders in council? I do not want the right to be extended indefinitely, but let us be given the opportunity for the first fifteen days of the next parliament to move to bring unfair orders in council before the house. I will give one example in connection with rentals as it affects men coming back from overseas. In two instances while the husbands were overseas the wives built houses, rented them and moved into small flats in order to earn a little extra income. Now that their husbands have come back they are denied the right to go into their own homes. When I got in touch with the rentals controller the answer I received was that it was thought to be in the public interest that the tenants remain. While I appreciate what the minister and the government have done in this bill and under lend-lease, there are certain questions which should be raised in connection with this bill. I have raised these matters in the house, often alone. The San Francisco agreement, the Bretton Woods agreement, the excise bill, our lend-lease-all these matters are interlocked and interrelated. We cannot discuss one without discussing the others and seeing the cause and effect. The
303S
Export Credits Insurance

United States abrogated lend-lease so suddenly that it left the mother country in a most dangerous position. She had lost her overseas investments and she was forced to revert back to the time when she was practically a small country.
This bill does not go far enough so far as the mother country is concerned. Last fall and again this spring I raised these same questions'. There is no use beating about the bush, there is no use shadow-boxing about this thing; there is no use just having window dressing; we must see what is in the window.
Let us see what is in the window at the present time. Up to Dunkirk the mother country was all alone except for the dominions. She had to borrow money in order to defend the United States shores. Lend-lease was one means for what purpose? It was to protect the United States shores. If it had not been for the protection given by the mother country, with the dominions, after France fell, New York would have been invaded as well as this country. The United States lend-lease bill as amended was good as far as it went, but for two and a half years they had a cash and carry policy.
The Minister of Finance has done quite well on behalf of the government with regard to the proposals concerning loans in this and in other ways for the mother country. I am sorry to see that some of the other parties in the house are not following the principle adopted by the late Mr. Fielding and Sir Wilfrid Laurier of preferential trade within the empire, in which I still believe-it will always be necessary. I believe some announcement should have been made long ago because the mother country does not know where Canada stands on trade, defence and migration. The Ottawa agreements were the greatest boon this country ever had. There are some matters I should like to refer to which may be out of order under this bill, as they were on Tuesday, but as long as discussion is allowed I think we have to discuss many things at the one time if we are to close the session in a few days.
I say, regardless of the merits of the proposals, that it is time the people knew where the empire and the dominions stand. At the present time we hear a great deal in this house from an internationalist and a leftist point of view. The government seems to be in a scramble to placate my hon. friends on the left. It reminds me of that first Easter Sunday when Peter and the other disciple had a race to the sepulchre and "the other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulchre." That is more or less the kind of thing that the government seems to be doing in relation to the "left" views expressed by hon.

gentlemen who, I may add, are quite friendly and very courteous in debate. I say that the government has not done its duty in failing to let the dominions know where we stand on the matter of empire trade, defence and migration within the empire. I am absolutely in favour of the Ottawa agreements and of empire trade, and not the less so after reading the debates which have been going on in the senate and congress at Washington.
What we call the Export Credits Insurance Act is a most commendable measure; I have only a few further remarks to make about it.
It is time for the government to lay all cards on the table, and to realize that the export credits bill, the Washington-Britain loan, empire trade, defence and migration within the empire are all wrapped up together; they all interlock. And what do we do? We sit here and fold our arms as a parliament. Influenced by waves of leftist propaganda and international sentiment, we seem to have forgotten all about the British empire, which guarded our shores and saved civilization, and which has been left to "carry the bag". Picture the situation of the mother country at the present time, and remember that, when lend-lease was discussed among the big three, it was understood that this assistance would continue for some time.
I do not think we have gone far enough in aiding the mother country in the matter of providing credits in exchange for goods and services. Also something should have been done for empire crown colonies and empire dependencies apart from the dominions. Take the case of the Fiji islands, whose tribes gave all they had and fought bravely for the empire in the recent war. Take the case of other dependencies and crown colonies whose soldiers, in the African campaign, marched across the desert under Montgomery and Alexander. Yet they have no part in the provisions of this credit bill. I say that some allowance should be made for any of these empire possessions which wish to come in.
My last point is that I believe we as a dominion should long ago have had a conference with the mother country on matters of trade and finance. There is a new government over there at the present time. In the last election the party they represent polled 11.000,000 votes and the Conservatives under Mr. Churchill received 9,000,000 votes, out of a total of 22.000,000 ballots, so the Conservatives were not very far behind.
I tell you this, that unless we as dominions stand by the mother country and get away from much of this internationalism and so-called collective security we shall live to ' regret it. Some of the results are reflected in the pacifism and leagues causing a second world war and resulting in the finan-

Export Credits Insurance
cial burdens of this country, the billions of dollars of war loans which have had to be provided by the taxpayers. In saying this I sympathize with the Minister of Finance, and I always have, in the good work he has done in his lend-lease and export credits act.
While I believe that the policy of lend-lease and export credits was right, and that it was a great patriotic move on the part of the government of the day, I think it should go farther. As for collective security, we have seen where that led to when Britain, in order to obtain a few ships, had to surrender bases. from Newfoundland down to British Guiana.
Let me reiterate that the time has come for the government to lay down its policy as regards the Ottawa agreements. They proved a great boon to this country. The mother country has been consistently our best customer, and it spent a lot of money developing this country. What are we going to do to-day? Apparently we are to enter into bargains in the name of internationalism with a number of different countries outside the empire, many of which were unfriendly to our country, and to do so by proposals and agreements made by ministers of the crown over the head of parliament. There should be a constitutional change which would prohibit ministers from entering jnto such agreements without reference to parliament. I say that course is entirely wrong. Unless the dominions and the mother country hang together they will hang separately. Historically, economically, geographically and financially our interests are one. The handwriting is on the wall, and the war will have been fought in vain unless these foundations are maintained. Only one-third of the proposed guarantees are before us in this bill; we should know something about the aggregate of loans to be made. The government must know all about the proposed United States loan to Great Britain; there was a debate on the subject in the British House of Commons and in the senate at Washington. The cause and the probable effects are well understood by them. I urge the government to give us more' information on these financial proposals and interrelated problems. Are we members just to be a lot of yes-men and nodders to endorse any proposals which the government put forward? I say no, and that it is the duty of the opposition to examine these policies and see how they are interrelated.
I appreciate what the government has done in this export credits bill. I believe the principle is right and should be extended. We should know whether any conference has been held with the new government in the United 47696-192
Kingdom with respect to the Ottawa agreements and preferential trade. Have any agreements or understandings been arrived at over there? If they have, it is the duty of the dominions to find out. If inter-empire trading arrangements are to go by the board it will be a sorry day for this country, because the hope of the world and of civilization is that the dominions and the mother country shall hang together. If they do they will have a powerful voice in the peace terms. Separately they are no match for Russia and no match for the United States, whether in the economic, the financial, the social or any other field. United they are more than an equal. If they hang together they are economically strong enough to get along without any other country. We can use our ports and harbours to transport our raw materials to the whole world, while maintaining our place in interempire trade. It is along such lines that we should be thinking. I am utterly opposed to much of this propaganda for trade and economic internationalism and so-called collective security. Such ideas, when put to the test, failed us years ago and will fail us in *he years to come, unless we take heed.
