subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to grant authority to accept on behalf of Canada and to carry out the obligations of Canada under the articles of agreement for an international monetary fund and an international bank for reconstruction ^nd development prepared by the united nations monetary .and financial conference held at Bretton Woods in July, 1944; to authorize the payment of the subscriptions required from Canada out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund to an amount not exceeding seven hundred million dollars; and to authorize the borrowing under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, of sums not exceeding seven hundred million dollars.
He said: In the measure now before it, the house is asked to express its approval of Canadian participation in the two new international financial institutions considered at the united nations monetary and financial conference held at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944. This conference was held after a couple of years of intensive discussion among the treasury officials of a large number of the united nations regarding the character and machinery of post-war financial relationships among countries. It was attended by the representatives [DOT] of forty-four nations and drew up proposed articles of agreement of an international monetary fund and an international bank for reconstruction and development. These articles of agreement are printed as a schedule to the present bill. The countries participating in the Bretton Woods conference were not committed to membership as a result of such participation: the proposed institutions come into being only after membership has been formally accepted by countries providing sixty-five per cent of the resources. The articles of agreement remain open for signature on the part of the countries which were represented at the Bretton Woods conference until the end of this year.
The proposed institutions are intended to be part of the permanent framework of international collaboration in the monetary field, though-as I shall endeavour to show later- they have a special significance in the difficult years that lie immediately ahead. The international monetary fund is primarily concerned with securing orderly exchange arrangements, while the bank is intended to help in the restoration of economies which have been destroyed or disrupted in the course of the

war and, over the longer period, to encourage and facilitate the international flow of capital for productive investment.
As members who have already had an opportunity of studying the proposed articles of agreement will, I am sure, agree, the subject matter is somewhat complicated. I do not propose at this stage to attempt to analyse the articles of agreement in detail, though I shall have something to say later about the salient features of the fund and the bank. What I should like to do now is direct attention to some of the more general considerations involved in these proposals.
The main issue which is at stake in the Bretton Woods proposals is the same as that involved in the united nations charter which this house recently approved by so over-w'helming a majority. That issue is: are we and other countries to organize and cooperate for peace, or is each nation going to use its strength and resources at the expense of others in a struggle for survival? In many parts of the world there is evident a keen awareness that if peace is to be maintained and if prosperity is to be achieved it will be necessary to plan for a higher degree of international collaboration than we have ever achieved in peace time in, the past. In pursuit of this purpose, the united nations are in-process of creating a number of institutions which are to serve a9 the instruments of such collaboration. The central institution is, of course, the united nations organization embodied in the San Francisco charter. This, it is hoped, will provide the political basis of security. But it is recognized that security also has an economic basis and that economic instability and poverty and unemployment provide a background conducive to political dissension among nations. More positively, all the experience of the past has demonstrated that it is only through collaboration with others that countries can hope, over a long period of time, to achieve real prosperity. Economic isolation in the modem world is as impractical a policy as political isolation.
It is for these reasons that the Bretton Woods proposals should, notwithstanding their technical complexities, be regarded as one part of the united nations effort to create and maintain a peaceful and prosperous world. On the political side, the keystone in the structure of institutions being set up for this purpose is the united nations charter. On the economic side we have, to date, three main pieces. There is UNRRA, the united nations organization to deal with urgent problems of relief and rehabilitation, which has received unanimous support from all sides of this house. There is the food and agriculture organization,

_______________Bretton Woods Agreements
which this house has recently endorsed and which lately held its first annual meeting at Quebec city. And there are t!he financial institutions discussed at Bretton Woods, whose long-run purposes are to help provide the monetary and financial conditions necessary for the sound and expansive development of international trade and to enable countries to cooperate with each other for this purpose without thereby lessening their ability to carry out domestic policies aimed at full employment for their own people. The structure of international collaboration will be by no means complete when the fund and the bank are established. These institutions do not look after the immediate payments difficulties of countries like the United Kingdom whose international financial position has been so weakened by the war. Nor does the establishment of a monetary framework conducive to liberal commercial policies in itself assure that liberal policies will in fact be followed. For this, separate agreement is necessary. I shall have more to say about these points later.
The objectives sought by the united nations through the establishment of these institutions are the same as those which we as Canadians seek for ourselves-expanded production, trade, employment and higher standards of living all round. The destruction and disorganization wrought by the war are so enormous that it is only through a cooperative effort that there is any hope of establishing normal conditions of trade within a reasonable length of time. We in Canada have happily escaped the physical destruction of war, but that does not mean that our participation in joint efforts to aid in the reconstruction of other countries is an act of outright generosity from wffich we shall get no material return. Quite apart from any moral obligations, the fact is that we need prosperous markets in the world if we are to be prosperous ourselves and we shall need the goods which these economies can sell us when they are reestablished once more.
The Canadian government and parliament have already recognized our responsibility and our interest in helping tide those with whom we have had a mutually profitable trade in the past over their immediate payments difficulties by making provision for direct and guaranteed loans in the Export Credits Insurance Act. The international bank for reconstruction and development will make and guarantee loans for the foreign currency requirements of reconstruction projects of the member countries. Through these two mechanisms, Canada is and will be contributing what it can to getting the war-devastated countries on their feet and getting production 47696-192J
and normal economic life started again. And in doing so, we are and shall be helping our own industries and farmers to find remunerative export markets and thereby to smooth the transition from the war to the peace economy.
From what I have said it is obvious that the Bretton Woods proposals are based in part on the immediate needs arising out of the war. But, significant though this element is, it is less significant I believe than the longer-run aspeets,of the proposals. As I have already indicated, the two institutions are regarded as part of the permanent machinery of international monetary collaboration. As such they are based on the experience of the inter-war period and they represent an attempt to avoid the errors of the past.
Members of the house will, I am sure, recall the disorganized state of international economic affairs that prevailed before the war. The international monetary standard that had been painfully reconstructed during the 1920's was built up by a piecemeal process in which each country chose its own time and its own rate for stabilization without regard to the effect of its action on others. The structure of exchange rates that resulted from the uncoordinated action of different countries was an irrational one which inevitably set up stresses and strains and weakened the system's resistance to shock. The overvaluation of sterling and the undervaluation of the franc are the most frequently cited examples. Another weakness of the system was that it did not provide adequate machinery for regular consultation among countries with a view to getting agreements on changes in exchange rates when changes were needed and with a view to getting agreement on coordinated policies aimed at economic stability. Further, there was no source of international credit to which countries had assured access. When the great depression struck, each country had to cope as best it could with the situation. For all, the prime consideration was to deal with unemployment, and the means of domestic recovery which appeared most practicable consisted of measures whose effect was to thrust the burden of the depression abroad. The result was the strangulation of world trade and the mutual impoverishment of all countries. The characteristic features of world economic relationships before the war were high and discriminatory tariffs, import quotas, export subsidies, depreciated currencies of uncertain value, discriminatory clearing agreements, multiple currency practices.
I am certain that in no quarter of the house is there a desire to see the world return to these pre-war practices. But if the nations
Bretton Woods Agreements

of the world are left to their own devices and are not bound together in an association of mutual advantage which will set certain standards for its members, they will in my opinion inevitably revert to the practices I have described. If we want a reasonable degree of orderliness and fairness. in international economic and monetary arrangements, we must set about to create it. It would bn idle to suppose that countries will embrace it automatically. There was a period in the modern history of the world when the international gold standard ensured order and stability in the international exchanges. At the present time, however, the house can be certain that there are very few countries which would be willing to adopt this standard and to tie their currencies rigidly to gold if that meant that they were thereby committed to abandoning from time to time domestic policies aimed at stability and employment in order to follow deflationary or inflationary influences originating abroad. This does not, of course, mean that they will not use gold as a means of international payment and hold it as a reserve against such requirements.
In practically all countries today the primary objective of economic policy is the maintenance of high levels of employment and production. No international monetary system, gold standard, Bretton Woods or any other, will be generally acceptable which is incompatible with this objective. The task is to harmonize the two objectives of internal stability and international cooperation, so that we can have not only high employment but also a high standard of living through the mutually profitable exchange of goods with other countries. For any international monetary system to endure, it is clear that the technical arrangements regarding exchange stability will have to be supplemented by other arrangements looking towards the prevention, through common action, of violent fluctuations in economic conditions.
The international monetary fund represents the united nations attempt to create agreed * arrangements to which all countries can adhere without feeling that they are entering a strait-jacket and to provide international monetary conditions that will be conducive to the expansion of international trade. The articles of agreement are the result' of intensive work on the part of the experts of forty-four nations over a long period of time. Inevitably they represent at certain points a compromise. No country was able to have each article drafted exactly as it might have wished, and I am not prepared to argue that the document is a perfect one or that experience will not prove

that changes are required. But I do say that the three or four key points in the fund proposal are a realistic and constructive attempt to deal with the main sources of difficulty in pre-war international monetary arrangements.
In the first place, the fund will be a permanent organ of international collaboration on monetary matters. It will be a forum at which problems of common interest to the members can be discussed before they reach critical proportions. This may seem simple enough, and indeed it is, but the fact remains nonetheless that before the war there was astonishingly little organized machinery for international consultation on these questions. The fund will be governed by a board of governors consisting of the representatives of each of the governments which are members. The governors will meet at least once a year and between meetings their authority as regards the day-to-day operations of the fund will be delegated to an executive directorate consisting of the representatives of the five largest countries and six to eight others elected by the remaining countries. It is not too much to hope that considerable benefit will be derived from these regular meetings, through those responsible for monetary and exchange policy in the various countries becoming familiar with each other's problems and being provided with frequent opportunities for working out solutions which will reconcile the interests of all.
The second main feature of the international monetary fund is that the nations joining it recoginze that exchange rates have more than purely domestic- implications and are therefore properly matters of international concern. Countries joining the fund agree on their initial rates of exchange and, apart from a leeway of 10 per cent, undertake not to alter them except after consultation with the fund. Competitive currency depreciation is out: members agree not to propose a change in their exchange rate except to correct a fundamental disequilibrium. These are the provisions designed to ensure exchange stability. But there are other provisions which are designed to ensure that this stability does not become rigidity and that countries will not be required as a result of their membership iq the fund to maintain an exchange rate which has ceased to be appropriate and which therefore involves them in economic dislocation. One of these is the provision which authorizes members to change the initially agreed rates by as much as 10 per cent without this requiring the concurrence of the fund. Another is the provision which imposes an obligation on

Bretton Woods Agreements
the fund to approve a requested change if the change is in fact necessary to correct a fundamental disequilibrium. The fund is specifically enjoined from concerning itself with the domestic policies-political, economic or social-which gave rise to the necessity for a change in the exchange rate to restore the economic balance of a country. It may only concern itself with the question of fact: is a change in the rate necessary to restore the balance or not? Thus the fact that a country has adopted a social security programme or has socialized its major industries can be no concern of the fund's if that member should subsequently apply for a change in its exchange rate: it cannot object on the ground that it disapproves of these measures and that they were responsible for the disequilibrium it is now desired to correct. If the disequilibrium in fact exists, the fund must agree to the change.
I do not think that it can be successfully argued that the provisions regarding exchange stability go further than it is desirable to go or that they represent an undue restriction on the liberty of action of the member countries. The undertaking that members give regarding exchange rates is an undertaking to consult: there is no undertaking to accept the fund's recommendations in all circumstances.
I have referred to two of the main features of the international monetary fund, namely the opportunity it provides for continuous consultation and the provisions it embodies regarding exchange stability. I come now to the third main feature, namely the provisions regarding exchange restrictions.
Members of the fund undertake, after a transitional period, not to impose restrictions on current account international transactions and to remove the restrictions now in effect as soon as conditions permit.
These provisions mean two things, both of particular interest to Canada. They mean that countries will not be entitled to discriminate against imports from any other mem-* ber on currency grounds and that the foreign exchange which a country earns as a result of exporting to any member of the fund will be available to be used to pay for imports from any other member of the fund. When these provisions are fully in effect the Canadian exporter will be able to compete in the markets of the world with the assurance that no special exchange restrictions will be placed in his way. There is to be no question of blocked accounts in respect of any current account transaction and Canada as a country will be under no pressure to use the entire proceeds of her exports to any particular country to buy imports from that particular
country. She will be free to use them to pay for imports from any part of the world. In other words, the international currency system which is being set up is one which permits of the multilateral clearing of balances resulting from international transactions. This is a matter of special importance to Canada on account of the structure of our balance of international payments, with its chronic surplus of sterling and chronic deficiency of United States dollars. The alternative of bilateralism, that is, the attempt to balance the trade between each pair of countries engaged in trade, was developed by Germany before the war and naturally proved [DOT] destructive of international prosperity. It is a system which, by restricting the area in which the proceeds of exports can be spent, necessarily results in worse bargains for the seller than if he had freedom of choice. It is a system, moreover, which lends itself to political abuse by enabling the strong to exploit the weak.
Unfortunately, the abolition of exchange restrictions on- current account transactions and the establishment of true multilateral clearing will not come into effect as soon as the international monetary fund is established. The immediate international financial position of certain countries is such that it will be necessary for them-unless other outside assistance is forthcoming on constructive terms-to continue for a period with exchange restrictions and clearing agreements of the type that have been in force during the war. This is notably true of the United Kingdom, which drastically curtailed her export trade during the war in order to devote all her productive effort to the war, Which lost a large part of her merchant fleet and her income from overseas investment and which incurred huge overseas liabilities for war purposes. It is also true of other countries, particularly those -which suffered years of systematic looting by the enemy. These countries will have import requirements far in excess of their immediate export capacity and it is recognized that the establishment of the fund will not relieve them of the necessity of husbanding their foreign exchange resources. Until a balance is established in the international accounts of these countries through reestablishment of their export trades or through other measures of outside assistance, it would not be reasonable to expect them to drop entirely their war-time exchange restrictions. They do agree, however, on joining the fund that this will be the objective of their policy towards which they will work as rapidly as conditions permit, and the fund is entitled to express views on any restrictions remaining in effect a few years after it is
Bretton Woods Agreements

established. And it is, of course, the case that the establishment of the fund contributes towards the speedier abolition of these restrictions both through the greater confidence which will result from the assurance of financial support and through its general effect in contributing to the expansion of world trade.
I should like to make it clear to members of the house that the exchange restrictions which countries joining the fund undertake to abolish refer exclusively to restrictions on current account transactions, that is, such things as payments for imports and interest and dividends on investments. There is nothing in the provisions of the fund which requires any member to abolish exchange restrictions on capital movements and it is recognized that in order to restrict capital movements it may be necessary to supervise and control all foreign exchange transactions. Far from prohibiting control of capital movements, the articles of agreement stipulate that the resources of the fund are not to be used to meet a large or sustained outflow of capital and that the fund may request a member to exercise controls to prevent such use of the fund's resources. Moreover, there is in the articles of agreement a positive provision to the effect that members may exercise such controls as are necessary to regulate international capital movements. I wished to make this explanation here in order to make it quite clear that an exchange control operated along the lines of our own at the present time is in no sense inconsistent with our undertakings under the provisions of the international monetary fund.
The undertakings which members of the fund give regarding exchange stability and the convertibility of their currency in respect of current account transactions are obviously important commitments. In return, members get the assurance that the fund will stand behind them in time of need. This brings me to the fourth and final aspect of the fund to which I propose to refer to-day, namely the fund's exchange operations.
Each member joining the fund is assigned a quota, which represents the measure of two things: its obligations to provide resources to the fund and its ability to draw resources out of the fund. The quotas of the countries-represented at the Bretton Woods conference were worked out there and printed as an annex to the articles of agreement. These quotas amount in the aggregate to $8,800 million. The United States quota is $2,750 million, the British 81,300 million, the Russian 81,200 million, the . Chinese, S550 million, the French 8450 million, the Indian 8400 million

and the Canadian $300 million. All the quotas are expressed in terms of United States dollars. The actual payments of tht^ subscriptions to the fund are, however, not in United States dollars but partly in gold and partly in the national currency of each member. The gold subscription is to be either 25 per cent of the quota or 10 per cent of the country's independent reserves of gold and United States dollars, whichever of these is less, with the balance payable in national currency.
The fund as originally constituted will therefore consist partly of gold and partly of national currency. It is believed that originally about $1,800 million of the fund's assets will consist of gold, and the balance of various national currencies. Members have the right to buy foreign exchange from the fund in amounts equal to their quota plus the amount of gold they originally subscribed. This right is subject to certain limitations of both a quantitative and qualitative nature. Thus, unless the fund waives this condition, purchases in any single year may not exceed 25 per cent of a member's quota, and a country having substantial international reserves of, its own must use these reserves to meet adverse balances to the same extent as it draws on its quota. Moreover, if the fund finds that a member is making use of its resources in a manner contrary to the purposes of the fund, it may, after due notice, suspend it from making further use of them. These provisions for exchange transactions with the fund are a very central part of the fund agreement. It will be seen that the fund's resources are a revolving fund, and international pool of credit which is available to member countries to meet adverse balances in their international payments and which allows time for adjustments to be made. It is this element of assured access to credits which provides the necessary flexibility in the system and which enables the countries adhering to this international standard to do so without fear that they are hereby entering a strait-jacket.
Under these arrangements, a country which suffers a temporary deficit in its balance of international payments due, say, to a crop failure at home or a recession in its. principal export markets, will know that it can draw on the fund to see it over the payments difficulties. It will therefore be relieved to that extent of the necessity of taking immediate steps to adjust its payments position -such steps, for example, as exchange depreciation, or import restrictions which would have a depressing effect abroad, or measures of internal deflation which would have a pressing effect at home. The knowledge

Bretton Woods Agreements
that the fund is there in cases of need should make countries more willing to use their own reserves to meet temporary deficits in their balances of payments. In short, by increasing the amount of international money, the international monetary fund introduces an important factor of flexibility which provides countries with the assurance that they will not, on each occasion of adversity, be confronted with the choice between cutting themselves adrift from the world economy or abandoning domestic policies aimed at high employment.
I believe that in these four points I have covered the highlights of the international monetary fund, though members will no doubt wish to have more detailed explanation of certain features at a later stage. I can deal with the international bank for reconstruction and development more briefly because, though it is no less important than the fund, it is less novel in conception.
I have already outlined the broad general purposes of the bank which are to aid in the reconstruction of war-devastated countries and in the development of economically backward areas. The bank is, of course, not intended to provide all, or nearly all, the capital required for these purposes. It is intended that private international investment should in due course supply the bulk of the funds required but it is recognized that for a while private investors in the creditor countries may hesitate to make foreign loans.
The bank is to have a capital of $9,100 million, subscribed by the forty-four countries represented at Bretton Woods. The subscription of each country to the bank is approximately the same as its quota in the fund. The Canadian subscription to the bank is $325 million. The subscription of each member is payable as to 2 per cent in gold and 18 per cent in national currency. The remaining 80 per cent of the capital subscription remains uncalled as a surety fund against obligations guaranteed by the bank or moneys borrowed by it. If it becomes necessary to call up unpaid capital in order to make good on an obligation of the bank, the call will be made proportionately on each member.
The bank will engage in activities of three types. First, it may make direct loans out of its own subscribed capital resources; second, it may guarantee loans raised through the private investment market; and third, it may make loans out of funds raised through the issue of its own obligations. Loans will be made or guaranteed only if the bank is satisfied that they increase the productive capacity of the borrower and are within the capacity
. of the borrowing country to service and each loan will have to be guaranteed by the government of the country in which the project is located or by the central bank of that country. The bank will charge a commission of 1 to 1| per cent on loans made or guaranteed by it.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Is that an annual charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
No; it is what is to be paid in initially. Eighty per cent of the capital is uncalled. Only twenty per cent is called,, and that is payable as to two per cent in gold and eighteen per cent in national currency.
As regards the original eighteen per cent of the capital subscription put up by each member in its own currency, this may be loaned by the bank only to make purchases within the country concerned. No such condition may be attached, however, to loans financed by the bank through the issue of its own obligations nor is the bank authorized to impose as a condition of its guarantee that the proceeds of a loan should be spent in the territory of any particular member or members. It should be noted, however, that the bank may borrow funds or guarantee loans only with the approval of the country on whose market the funds are raised. Outstanding loans made by and guaranteed by the bank may not exceed the unimpaired capital, reserves and surplus of the bank.
The most novel feature of the bank proposal is perhaps the way in which it recognizes that while only certain countries are in a position to lend abroad, namely those which have surpluses in their current account balance of payments, the process of foreign investment, through its effect in raising productive efficiency and living standard, is one from which all countries derive benefits-and that it is therefore right that all should share in the risks attached thereto. The risks involved in the bank's activities will be shared proportionately by all the participating countries since all will be called upon to make good any losses which occur.
I wish to turn now to the specific obligations of Canada under the fund proposals and their specific advantages to us. First, our financial obligations. Under the fund our quota is $300 million in terms of United States currency; we shall be required to put up $75 million in gold and the balance in Canadian dollars. To whatever extent the fund does not require Canadian dollars for its operations we may, under the articles of agreement, substitute non-interest bearing nonnegotiable notes redeemable at par on demand. The fund woiild require redemption of these notes only when other members had an excess of payments to Canada and there was a net

Bretton Woods Agreements
demand for Canadian dollars which the fund was called upon to satisfy. In these circumstances we should be obliged to raise funds to redeem the notes and a financial burden would arise. But it is important to note that the burden arises because we have a favourable balance of payments and not because we are members of the fund. Without the fund the favourable balance would give rise to accretions to our foreign exchange reserves which also would have to be financed. Or alternatively, if there were no fund, foreign countries might reduce their purchases in Canada because they were short of means of payment here. In that case our financing problem would be reduced but our economic problem would be aggravated.
The important thing for members to bear in mind is that the only thing that can happen to the Canadian dollars which we put into the fund is to be spent in purchasing goods and services in Canada. While they are being spent in this way and the fund's holdings of Canadian dollars are being reduced, we are in effect extending credit to foreign countries through the fund. But it is credit which need not remain outstanding any longer than suits us, for if we wish to take repayment in the only practical form, namely goods and services, we shall have an import surplus which we will be in a position to finance through the fund.
As for the non-financial aspects of the fund agreement, I venture to think that there are few countries in the world which have a greater interest in securing orderly exchange arrangements and expanding world trade on a multilateral basis than Canada. Foreign trade remains a most vital element in our economic system and it cannot prosper under conditions of widely fluctuating exchanges, blocked accounts and bilateralist and discriminatory trade and currency practices. The structure of our balance of payments, with our chronic surplus of sterling and chronic deficiency of United States dollars on current account transactions, is such that we must have multilateral clearing and b6 able to offset the one against the other if we are to prosper in this country. While the Bretton Woods proposals do not ensure multilateral clearing at once, they do hold out the best hope that has been offered so far that this will be adopted by all countries as their common objective to be achieved within a reasonable period of time. .
I should like to make a few general observations by way of conclusion. I think that the house, in considering these proposals, should have a proper appreciation of the ser-

iousness of the foreign situation and of the nature of the real alternatives to the general approach towards the organization of international economic relations represented by Bretton Woods. The economic systems of half the countries of the world have been turned topsy-turvy as a result of the war. Capital equipment of all sorts-roads, bridges, factories, transport systems-have been destroyed, rich farm lands have been inundated, millions of persons have been separated from their ordinary place of employment. Currency systems have been weakened by inflation. Production has been reduced to painfully low levels. The network of normal trade relationships built up over past years has been destroyed. With regard to parts of Europe there is such a complete black-out that we can only imagine the degree of economic disorganization.
Members of the house will have clearly in their minds the way in which the economic dislocations caused by the last war remained to plague us in the 1920's and 1930's. The extent of the dislocation this time is infinitely greater and anyone who believes that it will be possible to introduce order and prosperity into international economic relations in the present state of the world by'small, unimaginative measures is living in a fool's paradise. Generally speaking, the attempts the world has made in the past generation to maintain a functioning world economic system have been of the patch-work variety: the motto has been "too little and too late." Past experience is not a good enough guide as to what we should be dbing now because the experience of the past has on the whole been unsatisfactory. There is no use relying in 1945 on the expedients that were tried and failed last time. We have to base our policies not only on an appraisal of past experience but also on an appraisal of present requirements.
Bretton Woods is an attempt to organize international monetary cooperation on a national basis for the common good. I believe that it marks a great step in advance. But it is only one step and a great deal more than Bretton Woods will have to be agreed to if we are to make real progress. In particular, some means will have to be found of dealing on a constructive and imaginative basis with the transitional balance of payments difficulties facing the United Kingdom and other countries whose foreign position has been weakened as a result of the character and extent of their contribution to victory. I do not believe that there is any economic issue under discussion to-day which involves higher stakes than this problem. If the approach to

Bretton Woods Agreements
it is hesitant and inadequate, then the world can look forward with assurance to economic conflict and economic distress for a long time to come.
What will happen if adequate steps are not taken to deal with the transitional balance of payments problems? The countries whose economic systems have been disorganized and which are short of foreign means of payments will be obliged under the pressure of necessity to impose restrictive controls of every type on their foreign transactions. They will go in for restrictive import licensing and prohibitions, exchange discrimination and every sort of regimentation to keep their foreign expenditures, particularly of the "hard" dollar currencies, within the limits that they feel they can afford. They will do everything in their power to keep consumption of foreign goods from rising and will pursue policies aimed at national self-sufficiency. These measures will ' provoke retaliation elsewhere and we shall find ourselves treading the path of which we caught a glimpse in the 1930's. The main difference as compared with the 1930's will arise from the fact that the world's knowledge of the technique of restriction and retaliation has been considerably improved in the interval.
It is difficult to believe that countries like Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom will stand ready to risk this type .of development because they fail to grasp the magnitude of the issues involved or the grievous consequences of lack of imagination and courage. There is no question here of generosity or lack of generosity. All that is required is understanding of the direction in which their own long-term interests lie. For all these countries, that direction is an expanding world economy based on liberal and non-discriminatory principles. It would be a major tragedy to have this escape their grasp because it was felt that one month's war expenditure was too high a price to pay for economic peace.
I have not hesitated to paint a somewhat gloomy picture of the world outlook. I have felt conscious of a responsibility in asking the house to approve this measure, not to promise more from these institutions than they will be capable of delivering. Bretton Woods makes an important contribution to the solution of the problems confronting us but it does only .part of the job. Surely it is not too much to hope that with the knowledge gained and the experience acquired during the past twenty years, the countries whose policies are of decisive importance will this time approach the task of world economic reconstruction
with proposals which are on a scale commensurate with the problems involved. Surely it is not too much to hope that we shall not once more fall into the trap of "too little and too late."

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure I express the feeling of every hon. member when I thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) for giving us this interesting and comprehensive statement of this all-important question.
I think it is impossible to overstate the importance of this.
I have no desire to detain the house in discussing any of the technical features, because I understand from the minister that there may be an opportunity to do that later if the need arises, but I wish to make a few remarks on the general situation.
The terms "Bretton Woods" and "Dumbarton Oaks" have been thrown freely about the world now for a great many months. I suppose Dumbarton Oaks registered deeply in our minds because it was concerned principally and primarily with the question of trying to create a framework of a peaceful world. We have all in our own persons or the persons of our families and our friends understood during these last years what war is, and we were all desperately anxious that when the San Francisco conference met and gave approval to the proposals of Dumbarton Oaks it would succeed.
However, for reasons present in the minds of us all we have gone through months of disappointment; that is not a strong enough term, we have an overwhelming anxiety. We find ourselves on the verge, in the immediate aftermath of one war and having gone through anxieties which seemed greater than we could have imagined; in some ways we feel at the moment that we are facing even greater anxieties, because we are dealing with things which are largely unknown, unpredictable and almost beyond imagination, in their scope and power.
Now w^e have the other side of the approach to peace. As the minister very truly said, are we and other countries to organize and *cooperate for peace? We all agree that economic organization can do a great deal for peace. No doubt we all agree that it is because we organized ourselves so badly in an economic way in the years between the two wars that we fell into the second war. I suppose I would be making a correct statement if I said that what we are now trying to do through this agreement is to seek to avoid the cataract of unfortunate things-I was going to say disasters-that piled on us after the last war. Let us go over them briefly.
Bretton Woods Agreements

First, there was the terrible inflation in Germany, coupled with the tremendous credits from the United States to Europe, and, most illogically, the raising of the United States tariff-two things utterly inconsistent. We go on to later events in that dismal decade: the new German mark set up in 1924, the British pound overvalued in 1925, and that uneasy five years when we seemed to be having prosperity, at any rate, on this continent and when we could not foresee what was coming, although we should have been able to foresee it, because of the things the minister has already described. In 1929 or 1930 came another raising of the United States tariff, followed by our own 1930 tariff, which must have been very unpalatable to many who voted for it but which was in line with the times. In 1931 we had Britain going off the gold standard, a step precipitated by the series of disasters, the failure of the chief Austrian bank in that year, and then the welter which followed, culminating in the ill-fated world economic conference in 1933, and by no accident, accompanied almost to the very day by the appearance of Hitler in 1933. The world was ready for him; we had done a good job to prepare the world for him.
Now we are trying through this device, as the minister said, to organize ourselves at this time for peace. Do not let us be frightened by the technicalities-sometimes we think it is the jargon-of the language of foreign exchange and imagine that it is something which does not enter into the life of each one of us. I do not think it is an exaggeration, when one considers Bretton Woods, and that this financial arrangement is based on the presupposition that there will be trade arrangements-otherwise I think the minister will agree that it has no chance of life-for us to conclude that this proposed arrangement goes to the very root of the matter, and that if it should fail our prospect will be very gloomy indeed.
What is the prospect we would have? Let us make no mistake about the seriousness of it to every nation, perhaps more to our own nation than to any other. What is the alternative? We use the terms "multilateral" and "bilateral" trade. They are long and complicated words. The minister, I think, has helped to make them clear this afternoon. We know what multilateral trade is. We had it in the years before the war and, with it, a reasonable degree of prosperity. Nations as a whole through their trade arrangements did good to each other, whereas in the thirties each was seeking to do the maximum harm to the other, or at least taking steps which had that effect. As the minister has indicated, we 
may not have any doubt about the effects of bilateralism and in particular we need not have any doubt, if this Bretton Woods agreement fails, what will 'happen to us in a regionalized world dominated by the sterling and . the dollar blocs.
Let us be clear what the sterling bloc means to us. We do not fit into the sterling bloc, but most of our competitors are in it-the Argentine, the Scandinavian countries, Australia, New Zealand. Let us be realistic about this. It means that since they are in the sterling bloc they have all the advantages, which we have learned to know only too well, of trade which comes from common currency arrangements. The minister has emphasized that already, and not a bit too strongly. He has referred to the chronic situation which we had in the past of a surplus of sterling and a dearth of dollars.
If we look back we can see that the prosperity of Canada has been based upon and has presupposed intimate and extensive commercial relations between the United States and the United Kingdom. As far as I can see, we never have and never can have prosperity if that does not exist. So that is the meaning of bilateralism; that is what the sterling bloc means; that is what we face, as I see it, if Bretton Woods fails.
What is the other side? Bretton Woods, as the minister very truly said, is an attempt to create a world where we can continue in peace some of the cooperation we had in war. I know there is a certain amount of irony in talking about cooperation when we are also going to compete. But we have the two things side by side in sport; we have them in various other fields. Cooperation and competition are not so mutually exclusive as they sometimes appear. What do we seek in a new world economic organization? We seek a world where there can be at least as great a degree of freedom in trade as there was before the first world war. How is this to be achieved? There is, as I understand the situation, only one possible way of getting it. That is why we have been all watching, I suppose with almost feverish anxiety, what has been happening in Washington, hoping that the United States have learned at long last that trade is a two-way street, and that they cannot live alone economically any more than they can live alone politically. I hope that the announcement in the newspapers this morning, which "all of us were glad to read, is an indication that they are coming to that view, although we know we cannot count on it too confidently, because there are many there who have not yet been convinced. Nevertheless I think it is fair to say we can

Bretton Woods Agreements
assume that the conversations which went on at Washington, while primarily connected with finance, and while issuing in this agreement of which we have read this morning, did not ignore trade. It would be "the play without Hamlet" for a financial discussion to ignore trade, and I think we can assume, indeed we have been told day after day in the newspapers, that the vital principles of trade were, as they had to be, constantly considered at Washington. Therefore, while the agreement announced this morning does not include trade arrangements, I hope-indeed "hope" is not a strong enough word-I pray, in the interests of the whole world, and primarily of our own country, that it does mean that various broad considerations and agreements with regard to the future of trade have been accepted, and that this substantial loan is the first step in facilitating their operation.
What are the chances of this succeeding? We used to hear a great deal in the early - days about various technical proposals. There was the White plan, which we understood involved a substantial return to the gold standard; the Keynes plan, which leaned substantially against it because of the lesson Britain learned in going on the gold standard in 1925, and other things; and then our own Canadian plan, of which we heard something, and which came in somewhere between. At any rate, I believe that we have a remarkably encouraging prospect in the fact that forty-four experts agreed. That is a wonderful thing. I have scarcely ever seen four experts who could agree, and for forty-four to have come to an agreement was a great tribute not only to themselves but to their belief in the seriousness of the problem which they were discussing.
Now there is an agreement and the Minister of Finance comes and asks us to approve it. I suppose some people will say, can we afford this large amount of money? My answer is that we cannot afford not to afford it. I say that because in my opinion-and I wish to avoid repetition-our position in this country is at present one of very great danger. I say that at the risk perhaps of repeating what I have said before, but I shall be brief about it. I say that this country has prospered bnly when we have had comparative freedom of trade and export. We are a country that has specialized. What have we specialized in? In wheat, in nickel, in aluminum, in newsprint and I suppose in a dozen other things which I cannot think of at the moment. What does that mean? It means in plain words that we produce a great deal more of these things than we can consume.
Take first of all the question of wheat. If I may, I would remind the house of what I said the other day, and I was sayng only what a hundred other people have said. When we talk about the internal reorganization of our own economy we should ask ourselves ' first of all since we can only consume 25 per cent of our own wheat what we are to do with seventy-five per cent of the people who grow wheat. I will not pursue that. I wish, however, to make the position clear. That is what I mean by saying that if we cannot have multilateral trade the prospect for this country is indeed bleak.
I come therefore to this position. I have tried to indicate what in my opinion is involved, the two alternatives. Multilateral trade means primarily that the United States is prepared to take a different tariff attitude.
I speak of the United States because that country is so much bigger than the rest of us, and I hope that the people of the United States have at last realized that even they cannot prosper without foreign trade and are therefore prepared to cast their bread upon the waters and that they are prepared to do so not only so far as Great Britain is concerned, but for the good of others as well, because China needs rehabilitation and the world needs rehabilitation;.and so far as I can see, unless peoples are prepared to face a drastic reorganization of their economies, unless we in Canada are prepared to contemplate such a drastic reorganization. I see no hope for prosperity in this country of the kind that we have had and the kind that we shall not have again until we have multilateral trade. I say no more about the sterling bloc. That is the alternative.
I now come to a few comments on the present situation. I should like to say what I think of certain aspects of our own action. For the last three months negotiations have been going on at Washington and they have been fraught with tremendous importance to us. The aim was to see whether the United States, the great "have" country, the great natural-resource country, the great financial country, was prepared to take steps which would enable Great Britain to see its way to adherence to the Bretton Woods agreement; for, as I understand it, if Great Britain does not adhere we shall not get the sixty-five per cent and the thing will not click.
As indicated by the Minister of Finance, and as indicated in the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) yesterday, we have stood by. I have no intention of becoming controversial, but I wish to point out one or two things
Bretton Woods Agreements

which, in my opinion, have some substance in them. I think it is a great pity that we felt that we had to stand by in these last three months. I have seen various statements from competent people, one of them appearing in a responsible paper a day or two ago, another being that very statement which the Minister of Trade and Commerce read yesterday, with reference to the heavy and indeed the- disastrous import restrictions which Great Britain has felt it necessary to impose upon us by reason of the scarcity of dollars. The statement to which I have reference is that the alleviation of these restrictions will depend upon the amount of financial assistance coming from abroad. They did not say the United States; they said "abroad", and that was interpreted, and I believe rightly interpreted, by a competent commentator as meaning the United States and Canada. That is what I believe the word meant, and that is what I think anyone would presume it to mean.
It has been very unfortunate that we have not been in trade consultation during the last three months, but I think I know the answer. The answer made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was that we had to await the outcome of the United Kingdom-United States conversations. Personally, I do not accept that explanation; I do not think that was necessary. I believe we made a mistake in that regard and I hope it is not a costly mistake. At any rate, I wish to say this.
I want to go back to one comment I made a day or two ago in this house, namely, that there is great danger that in these negotiations we may rely too much on meetings of experts behind green doors.
I am not decrying the experts. No one has a greater belief in them than I have. But I suggest earnestly that there is grave danger of the public being kept out of their own business. I am not suggesting that you can make a trade treaty by having a debate. I am not suggesting that at all; I have enough sense to know that it cannot be done. I suggest, however, that this trade situation with Britain has been tense. In fact, we all know that it is. Tenseness is' in the air, and now we have this sudden action by Britain. Apparently it was sudden because Mr. Attlee did not seem to know about it when he was here. The situation, at any rate, has resulted in these sudden restrictions which Great Britain has imposed.
I do not blame them; maybe there was no other way out. But the public was taken by surprise, and I am not at all sure that the responsible officials and the ministers were not also taken by surprise. Certainly, we the public, were taken by surprise.

I suggest that this is a case where public opinion should have a chance to express itself. I believe that the people of Great Britain realize the part that Canada has played with them. I am not suggesting eleemosynary arguments; not at all. I believe that the people of Britain have a great feeling against regionalism, and I think that if they had had a chance to know the situation it would have been better. It would have been better if we had seen fit to debate the matter 'in this house, but instead we have been sitting here for three months, not always profitably occupied. Had we seen fit to debate the matter, some good might have been done.
I am not overlooking the fact that in April the government issued a white paper in which they enunciated what seemed to me to be a wise attitude toward foreign trade; but that does not seem to me to be the same thing as having a debate in this house, taking the views of the house, having the press of the country express its views, and having the public apprised of the situation. I think the public was taken terribly by surprise when the thing happened a week ago. The people were inclined to feel harshly about it. I did until I pulled myself up and began to realize the situation. But when you read the memorandum which the Minister of Trade and Commerce submitted to the house yesterday you cannot blame them. You can only say, why was not something done about it?
Well, was there nothing that could be done to prevent it? My contention is that there was something that could have been done, and I repeat, it is a pity that in these last ' three months we have not been in negotiation. Maybe that part can be remedied, but I seriously suggest that there is force in the other point I made, that, after all, the people primarily interested in this are the public in Canada and in Great Britain.
Experts have their place, and it is an important place too.
Looking back on it I am not able to see why it would not have been possible tq have the policy enunciated. I asked the minister the other day whether our policy was formed.
I think he said "no." I asked him whether our policy in this matter should not be formed, and again, as I recall it, he said "no." I am coming back to that and asking-and this is really my last point-whether it is not possible even yet for the minister to give us- without disclosing any secrets, or invading the field of the experts-an opportunity before the house prorogues, to discuss this matter, which is literally a matter of life and death to us.

Mr. Speaker, I think in all probability the resolution which is now before us, and the bill which the resolution foreshadows, may be one of the most important matters which have come before this house in many a long day. My colleagues and I do hot want to be in the position of voting for such an important agreement unless we are absolutely familiar with its broad principles and probable effects. Therefore I am hoping that the minister will carry out, and I believe he will, the proposals that have been made in this house not only by myself but by others that the bill will go before the banking and commerce committee where we can get the expert opinions that the experts have expressed elsewhere, regarding this matter and that they will give us the benefit of all the opinions, know-ledge and advice'which we can get. speechtext:
I agree that that ought to be done. I intend to move that the bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee. I would hope it would be given second reading and referred. I do not think the house loses any rights in doing that.
Mr.-COLDWELL: No; as long as we have the assurance that this bill will be referred to the committee we are not going to oppose this rfesolution. That is the understanding I want to give the minister and the house at this time.
I recognize, as did the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, and the minister when he introduced this measure, that we are faced with international chaos unless we can build some international system- which will- not only
Bretton Woods Agreements
prevent future war, but prevent economic conditions from arising which will make future war more or less inevitable, and these conditions often arise. I am not going to say they always arise, because I do not intend to enter into an argument regarding the influence of economics and social developments on war, although I have a point of view regarding that matter. I merely cite it as one of those sets of conditions that from time -to time seem to lead to war.
I was present, as a delegate at the San Fraqcisco conference, and I am grateful for that experience. I know the difficulties of obtaining consent from sovereign nations to anything which may seem to impinge upon their sovereignty. If I may add this other personal experience, only last week-end I attended a conference which I considered to be perhaps even more fascinating, and to some extent more instructive and certainly more terrifying than the great conference I attended at San Francisco; At the conference" I attended in New York last week-end I had an opportunity of listening to scientists, many of whom had studied and developed atomic energy and produced the atomic bomb. I wish to say that those scientists, not politicians, came to the conclusion that many people in the political lives of our countries are being driven to, namely, that somehow or another, and as rapidly as possible, we must build a world organization which will be able to give mankind government at the international level, in order to solve the great problems of peace and war which might arise in the future.
It is quite true, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said a few moments ago, that world trade channels and conditions have changed considerably in the last quarter of a century. One reason that makes me desire, perhaps more than any other, to get a clear view of what this means is that in effect I believe we are to a large extent under this agreement linking our own fortunes as a nation and the fortunes of the world to the economy of the United States.
Before the great war, Great Britain was the principal trading nation of the world. She relied upon what was called the unfavourable balance of trade, which enabled her to make tremendous purchases overseas and to receive goods produced in every part of the world, and which gave her what appeared to be an adverse balance of imports over exports. Then the world producers were able to find outlets for the goods which they produced. But that has all been changed by two wars, and to-day we are in a very different position. The nation which to-day con-
Bretton Woods Agreements

trols, shall I say-and I am not sure of my figures in this regard-practically half the great capital assets of the world-I did not say "owns" them; I said "controls" them- and is in receipt of the highest national income many times over is the United States. After the first great war we saw the United States, having become a great creditor nation, refusing to accept the obligations of that position. She refused to accept the imports that were vital to the welfare of the rest of the world. Consequently to-day we wonder if there has been a change in the conception of international trade and if the United States is prepared to do what is necessary in order that the nations of the world may trade, and trade with her. In reality is she prepared to receive payments in the only form in which payments can ultimately be made, namely, in the form of goods and services? If she is, I think the complexion which may be placed upon this Bretton Woods agreement is a much more optimistic one than we might otherwise think.
We have to bear this in mind: When I say this about the United, States, let us remember that Canada, too, is a creditor nation, and the policy which our country must follow is that of agreeing to international trade. I think that was implicit in the remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, who is sitting with a party which has been historically a high-tariff party, but which to-day, if we can follow what the hon. member said, is prepared as a party to revise that point of view fundamentally. If that is so, I believe that it will be a good thing for our country. Indeed, if we can reach the unanimous conclusion that Canada is in favour of receiving payments in goods for the commodities that we export, and we use our imports to improve the standards of life of our own people we shall progress. After all, it seems to me the only object of trade is to assure results that are mutually advantageous to all who trade. If the trade of Canada is to be mutually advantageous, then the exports we send abroad must be paid for by the receipt of some things in return; and those some things, if I may adopt that phraseology, must be used not for the enrichment of a small group of people but to raise the general standards of living for all. On that basis international trade is sound and acceptable.
I have just glanced at the evening newspaper. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario did not have that advantage; it was brought into the chamber whileihe was speaking. I am glad to note, and it makes me feel a little easier about this agreement, that if unofficial dispatches from Britain can be be-

lieved, as I think in all probability they can be believed in this instance, there is great hope that the United States will cooperate with Britain and the rest of the. world in freeing the channels of trade to a large extent, and reducing those tariff barriers that bedevilled the world prior to the war. If that is so, then Canada as a great exporting nation must also assume her proper place as a great ' importing nation and use the imports we are able to get for the produce we export to increase our standards of living.
But I would not want to leave my thought at that, Mr. Speaker, because I think we have to look beyond our own selfish, nationalist point of view and the good of our own people. I remember one evening at San Francisco the statement was made that before the war two-thirds of the population of the world, that is two persons out of three, never had a sufficient amount of food with which to fill their stomachs day by day. That was not during the war, remember, but before the war. I believe that in a Christian civilization such as that in which we boast we live we must pay some heed to these other countries. Therefore I hope and trust that in this B;-etton Woods agreement, when we come to study it, we shall find ways and means of enabling the areas of the world where these conditions exist, which we sometimes call the backward regions of the earth, to raise their standards of living. If we do so, then we make our own standards of living more secure, because no nation and no group of people can keep up their standards of living permanently if a very large portion of the world remains on much lower standards. So that as far as this agreement seeks to achieve that end-and that is the problem I want to see investigated to some extent when this bill is before the committee-it hiay be very worthy of our support, but I want to know about that before I say that the agreement will receive our support.
Since the bill is going to committee I do not think there is very much more I wish to say now. I really rose to ask the minister the question which he answered. I am glad to have [DOT]that answer, and I hope that when we go into this bill the doubts we may have in regard to tying the world to the United States dollar or the United States economy or the modified gold standard will be resolved. Perhaps I should say that I know this is not tying the world to the gold standard as we knew it in days gone by, because the factors entering into this agreement are not the gold standard factors. My understanding of the old gold standard was that a nation's currency had a fixed -value in terms of gold, that its currency

Bretton Woods Agreements
was always interchangeable in 'terms of gold and convertible into gold on demand. This agreement, I know, does not restore that. The old gold standard compelled each nation to allow gold to move freely between itself and all other nations of the world. We do not have that here, but as the minister indicated we have something else. This agreement is in two parts. I am not going into them, although I had intended to do so if this had not been going to committee. The first part has to do with the stabilization fund, and incidentally it has been interesting to me to see where the opposition has come from in regard to this Bretton Woods agreement. The stabilization fund has been strenuously opposed by the American bankers' association. They do not like it because it places some three billion dollars ini an international pool over which the American bankers' association really will have no control. On the other hand, the more progressive elements in the world have favoured the stabilization fund. As far as the international bank is concerned, the American bankers' association and other bankers do like it, because it is more orthodox and they perhaps understand its implications and intend to use that bank for their own advantage, whale the more progressive elements have not liked the idea.
