speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) for the only really intelligent speech on this measure this afternoon. That may sound an extreme statement, but I believe the investigations of the committee will prove the truth of much of what the hon. gentleman said.
May I refer for a moment to the remarks of those who have already spoken. The Minister
of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) gave us an excellent dissertation on the subject and presented the case for the Bretton Woods agreement just about as admirably as	it could be
presented by the most highly skilled experts in the world. I presume he had the assistance of the very best available experts in preparing his speech. May I refer to the various things he said? In the first place, he wisely acknowledged that economics are a fundamental cause of war. Let us in this house never forget that for a moment.	If we are to
remove war from the world we must remove the economic cause of war; and fundamentally the economic cause of war is not various modifications and manipulations of a nation's money but the fact that some nations are unable to sell as much goods as they need to buy. That applies to all nations likely to be debtor nations. The other nations are able to sell far more than they buy, and they become creditor nations. The difficulty which confronts the world at this time is to achieve some equalization between such countries as the United States, with its colossal productive capacity, and such countries as Britain which, because of the exhaustion of war, finds itself in an abject position from the point of view of productive potential.
The minister said another thing which is entirely worthy. He said the main issue before us is peace. I agree. And I think this house will discover that the main objection to Bretton Woods is that there is not a single phrase in it which by any kind of interpretation can mean any move toward peace in the world. As a matter of fact, it is one of the most complete and perfect guarantees of which the mind of man can conceive, that there will be war.
The minister mentioned institutions which were to be used, and referred particularly to the united nations charter. I am not going to discuss that. We will take his word upon it.
Then he turned to the economic aspect of the world situation, and told us that thus far w<* have three measures which are designed to solve the economic problems of the world. He named UNRRA, the food and agricultural organization and Bretton Woods. I am glad he named those, because by naming them he proved the absolute mental bankruptcy of the men who provide the whole set of measures which are proposed to be used to guarantee peace; for there is not a single thing in any one of the three of them, or in all put together that will overcome the fundamental economic difficulties which confound the world at the present time.
Bretton Woods Agreements
:ommons
He said that we need prosperous economies in the world. True. Bretton Woods will not produce prosperous economies. Bretton Woods will produce absolutely ruined economies everywhere in the world, except in the United States, Canada and Russia.
He* mentioned export credit arrangements. Yes, but export credit arrangements only put nations more deeply into debt, and the thing which is destroying them at the present time is unrepayable debt.
He mentioned that Bretton Woods is designed to be permanent. That is a warning to us. He gave us the outline of the features which were involved in Bretton Woods-four of them-and I shall not refer to them in detail. He painted a - gloomy picture-yes. But one does not clear away the gloom in a picture by talk, even if the talk is in Bretton Woods.
The minister has said that Bretton Woods does only part of the job. I ask the minister, and I think the house must demand that the minister show us who and what are to do the rest of the job, and how it is to be done. That does not at the present time appear in any proposal before the house.
For a few moments I should like to refer to what was said by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). I wish he were in the house, because he needs a lot of instruction. He, too, talks about a gloomy picture. Once more may I point out to him that he cannot clear up a gloomy picture by talking about it. He must find some way or another by which he can enable debtor nations to pay their debts, remembering they can pay ' their debts only in goods or services. How in the world can they pay their debts to a nation like the United States,. if the United States stubbornly refuses to accept their goods? That she is likely to do exactly that, one may reasonably conclude from the fact that she persistently refused to accept goods in repayment of the debt which Great Britain had to carry as a result of the last war. And the United States was not even honest enough to tell her own people what the situation w#s. She led her people, almost the whole rank and file of them, to believe that Britain had dishonoured her debts when, as a matter of fact, the United States had dishonoured Britain's debts by putting up tariff barriers which prevented Britain's goods from entering the United States.
Is there anything in Bretton Woods which will overcome a thing like that? Is there anything which will cause any ordinary man, any ordinary elector in the United States to allow the administration of that country to

make a change in policy such as would be necessary in order that they might accept goods from Great Britain? These are questions which hon. members must ask themselves, and must insist that the minister answer.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario speaks about destroying the sterling bloc. He did not exactly say that he advocated destroying it, but I gathered from the general purport of his remarks that he favoured the destruction of the sterling bloc. Well, what is it there for? It is there to protect a number of these debtor nations. And one of the fears we need to have about Bretton Woods is that it is designed to destroy the sterling bloc.
The question we must ask is this: How is the sterling bloc to protect itself if Bretton Woods does destroy its defences? Not a word is said as to how that is to be done. I challenge the minister or anyone else to show in Bretton Woods a single line which indicates how the sterling nations would protect themselves if the sterling bloc were destroyed.
He asks: What does it mean to Canada? Well, we will grant that we Canadians would like to have the' sterling bloc destroyed, perhaps, so that Canada might dump her goods, and have members of the sterling bloc more and more deeply plunged in irrepayable debt to Canada.
In the last analysis, what good would that do us? These are things we have to look at. It is purely an economic problem.
The minister should ask himself, and all hon. members ought to ask themselves what will happen to Britain and what will happen to these other members of the sterling bloc if something is not done to change the economic attitude of the creditor nations of the world. He spoke of the trade street being a two-way street. I thought the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) did admirably when he pointed out that if trade is to be a two-way street for the United States she must take measures to see to it that she imports goods, where necessary, to pay for the goods she exports. I think one could look all through United States papers and through the statements of United States public men and see absolutely no indication of any determination to change. The people of that country simply will not allow their administration to accept goods-beef and other commodities-which will compete with their own. This means that it is impossible for the United States administration to change their attitude.
At the same time, if we introduce Bretton Woods, as the United States has clubbed Great Britain into accepting Bretton Woods, we shall destroy utterly the means of protec-

Bretton Woods Agreements
lion, which is the only thing left to those debtor nations. It is true that trade must be a two-way street. But the nations in the world that are able to make it a two-way street are such as the United States and Canada. Other nations cannot do so. Therein I say, lies Canada's greatest responsibility, as we face this whole Bretton Woods question.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario spoke about Canada's specializing in wheat. We grant that she has specialized in wheat; we grant that she has specialized in dozens of other things. But the impressive thing about Canada is that while she has specialized in wheat and other primary products, she also proposes to specialize in the production of automobiles, agricultural implements, textiles and a great many other commodities. We know that Canada is not prepared to accept those commodities from Great Britain or any other country, with the result that it is more and more difficult for her to accept goods in return for those she wishes to sell. The same is true of the United States.
One of the noteworthy things about the United States is that she is almost self-sufficient. I do not mean absolutely, but certainly in a large measure tha*t is so. Canada, too, is capable of being largely self-sufficient. The more capable a country is of being selfsufficient, the more reluctant it is to allow goods from another country to enter its market; and the more it is in a posiiton to forbid the entrance of those goods.
If the United States and Canada are really honest in this whole matter, then the very first thing they will do is to bring down their tariff barriers and say, "We will accept so much goods, and so many other things." Then Great Britain may take more comfort. But merely to say they wall, and at the same time to want Great Britain to sign on the dotted line is one of the most callous and wicked things any nation in the history of the world has ever done.
That may be strong language, but while I am on that subject I shall say a word or two more. I shall have something m,ore to say about the United States before I have finished. I have noticed that since 1942 there have been appearing in the ordinary periodicals of the United States outlines of the terms of victory or conquest they were going to dictate to Great Britain. One would think that the people who caused the war, who attacked the other nations, was Britain. The terms they were going to dictate to her were simply terrible. Here we have one of them-Bretton Woods. This is one of the terms dictated by a conquering nation upon a helpless, conquered foe-Britain. Britain, which as we all
know stood and defended Americans, is to be crucified by a callous administration not knowing what it does. That is what we see today. That is what we see in the statement from Washington to-day. Think of a noble nation like Britain clubbed into a position which she knows herself means her utter economic destruction. Then to have the Minister of Finance of the elder dominion in the empire advocate in this house, that Canada, eldest daughter in the British family, pick up the club and go and help the United States beat the motherland to death. That must be comforting news for the empire's centre, ail in one day!
I should like to turn just briefly to the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I have no criticism to offer of his speech, but I wish to point out I believe there is in the mind of every hon. member who is doing me the honour to listen to me, as so many are, a stirring question, "What in the world are we going to do?" Do you favour having Canada discontinue the manufacture of agricultural implements, for example, so that we can import them from Britain? Do you favour Canada discontinuing the manufacture of shoes so that we may import them from Britain? '

speechtext: Or sugar?

speechtext:
You could go right down a long list, and I judge that the answer from practically every hon. member would be "no." The member for Lethbridge says "no" also. Then the question arises: What are we going to do? What can the United States do? The lease-lend arrangement showed what can be done and tbe Mutual Aid arrangement which Canada used for years showed what can be done. These people will say, "You surely do not favour our embarking upon a policy of perpetual gifts to the nations abroad, do you?" May I refer to the words of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and I hope he will correct me if I have not their sense correctly. He said that trade should be mutually advantageous; that it should be a blessing both to him who gives and to him who receives. Surely selling wheat to Britain which puts Britain into an Prepayable debt position to Canada is a blessing only to Canada; it certainly is not a blessing to Great Britain. I agree that trade should be placed on a new basis. In order to understand how it can be put on a new basis, we shall need to revise our financial thinking.
I am not going to discuss the financial principles which are advocated by this group, but I am going to lay down as a sort of general
Brctton Woods Agreements

challenge at the present time for hon. members to be thinking about for the next two or three days., this problem: You tell me how the problem can be solved, unless you can learn how to finance Mutual Aid and lease-lend arrangements in perpetuity without creating debt and increased taxation for the nation. If you cannot find out how to do that without social credit, may I suggest that you promptly study social credit.
I had intended to say some other things. Possibly I had better say some of them. All these matters were just the result of my reflections when I heard some of the remarks, the desolate, gloomy and hopeless remarks, made by the first two speakers. As this house proceeds to deal with the Bretton Woods proposals involved in this resolution, parliamentary government itself is on trial. This particular Canadian parliament is on trial. The question is raised whether we are capable of finding a solution in this our darkest need; whether we are capable of clearing away the smoke-screen obstruction which has been built up to hide from us the essential features of Bretton Woods and then reject the thing as we ought to do.
On the<tlay that Canada accepts the Bretton Woods proposals she locks upon her limbs the fetters of perpetual bondage; she betrays her trust to the 650,000,000 people of the British commonwealth and empire. She fails mankind in the world's hour of desperate need. I think what I have said already indicates the truth of what I say there.
The Bretton Woods proposals centre around two main features, as the minister has pointed out. First, there is the international monetary stabilization fund, the governing body of which is galled the fund. Second, there is the international bank ostensibly set up-mark you, I said "ostensibly", and it is true-to lend money to needy nations to aid them in rehabilitating themselves.
The international monetary fund agreement is merely a device for tying up the currencies of the world to the United States dollar based on gold. The fund agreement is merely a device for forcing the world to borrow and use the huge masses of United States gold now lying idle and worthless in United States vaults. That is all it is fundamentally. This agreement is purely a mechanism for bringing the nations of the world, except Russia, humbly and helplessly, cap in hand, to beg the right to live at the feet of the little gang of questionable characters who now hold the title deeds to the gold of the non-Russian world. They have $23 billion of it down there in the United States. It is no good at all; they
tMr. Blaokmore ]
do not know what to do with it. This whole Bretton Woods thing is a scheme to put that idle gold to work.
The fund is a mechanism for binding the moneys of all the nations to the United States dollar. The United States dollar is and will be based on gold; it is tied immovably to gold. The supply of United States dollars will be completely controlled by the federal reserve system of the United States, and the federal reserve system is utterly controlled by the holders of United States gold. The setup under Bretton Woods will be perfect for the holders of gold. And those gentlemen in the main are international financiers. I would ask you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, perhaps the house will permit me to make a statement regarding the agreements that have been reached in the economic and financial discussions between the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States. The statement was made by those two governments at half-past five this afternoon. I have long teletype messages which I have not had time to read, but the effect of them appears to be about as follows.
These governments have made public this afternoon the text of a financial agreement between the two governments under which the government of the United States proposes to extend a line of credit of $3,750,000,000 to the United Kingdom on terms which are specified therein. They have also made public the text of a joint statement regarding settlements for lend-lease, reciprocal aid, surplus war property and other claims of the two governments arising out of the conduct of the war for which an additional loan of $650,000,000 is provided. The secretary of state of the United States has made public a document setting forth certain proposals for consideration by an international conference on trade and employment, and the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom have made a joint statement regarding their understandings on the proposals of commercial policy set forth in this document. The proposals have the endorsement of the executive branch of the government of the United States, and the government of the United Kingdom expresses its full agreement on all important points in these proposals and accepts them as a basis for international discussion. The two governments have announced that they will begin preliminary negotiations at an early day between themselves and with other countries, for the purpose of developing concrete arrange-

Bretton Woods Agreements
merits to carry out these proposals, including definitive measures for the relaxation of trade barriers of all kinds.
As I have already said, I have not yet had an opportunity of reading these documents. I do not propose to make any comments upon the substance of them, but I wish to say that I welcome and I think that this house will welcome the fact that Britain and the United States have reached agreement, both on these financial matters and on the basic principles and methods of approach to the reduction of trade barriers.
While I have not had time to read the proposals on commercial policy, they have resulted from discussions among officials that have extended over two or three years, in some of which our officials have participated, and I am happy to see them put forward as the basis for general consideration and action.
Copies of the documents have been received and will be made available, in convenient form, to the house next week; perhaps before that, if I can arrange it.

Mr. Speaker, before the house took recess I was dealing with the matter of Bretton Woods. The things which I had to say concerning the importance of Bretton Woods and the effect of it upon the world would lose meaning, I believe, unless I brought some evidence to show that the Bretton Woods agreement involves the gold standard. May. I read a quotation from an article reprinted by kind permission of the Daily Express from Britain of Thursday of August 10, 1944, by Paul Einzig, author of "Currency after the War." He is one of the greatest authorities on money and finance in the world to-day. The title of his article is: "1925 and All That, Only Far, Far Worse. A Plain Man's Guide to the Menace of Bretton Woods." The excerpt I desire to read is as follows:
Yet, once the plan is translated into intelligible English and is denuded of all camouflage, every layman of normal intelligence is bound to realize that it is the gold standard, the full gold standard and nothing but the gold standard.
Admittedly, it is a different gold standard from the one we abandoned in 1931, just as the gold standard adopted in 1925 was different from
the one suspended in 1914. But the changes are, for the most part, considerably for the
worse.
Then he gives five reasons to support his contention, which reasons later in the debate will be listed for the consideration of the [DOT] house. I believe we are safe in assuming that the proposals of Bretton Woods mean the return to the gold standard. Once under Bretton Woods, the greatest nations would be mere doormats for the dirty feet of the international financiers.
What the world needs is not so much monetary stabilization as trade stabilization, trade equalization. By this I mean that any given nation-France, Holland Belgium, any given nation-shall be free to repay with goods for the goods which it buys. 3lso that any given nation in the world, if it is unable to produce the raw materials which it needs, or unable to manufacture the goods which it needs to exchange for the goods which it requires from abroad, shall be free to obtain goods surplus in other nations on a lend-lease or mutual aid basis, so that the high-sounding ideals expressed in the Atlantic charter may become realities, and that a nation shall be literally free from fear and want.
Once these two conditions are observed in the world, then we can have trade equalization, that is to say, a condition in which any given nation shall be able to pay for the goods which it requires from abroad with goods of its own. Without trade stabilization, trade equalization. Continued increase in world trade, except for the United States, is impossible; rising world standards of living are impossible; freedom from want and fear is impossible; and freedom of religion and of speech will soon become impossible.
Monetary stabilization can be obtained by voluntary' conversations, understanding and conventions. There need not be any overruling, all-powerful central dictatorship with power of life and death over whole states. National money can be stabilized upon price indexes of goods. This principle has been well illustrated in what has been called managed money during the past decade. The same principle can be used to obtain international currency stabilization. Once trade is equalized and stabilized, no nation would think of allowing its money to fall out of step with the world's monetary procession. No nation would have any reason for getting out of step, for the only reason why nations get out of step to-day is that they find themselves unable to pay with their own production for the goods which their people are buying from abroad. They therefore adopt monetary devices for their own protection. Any nation would have every reason for keeping in step
Bretton Woods Agreements

if trade were stabilized. Having plenty of productive capacity to supply all its needs, any nation would be able to stabilize its price level by four simple devices, all of which have been illustrated to the house: first, plenty of production; second, price discounting with compensation; third, price subsidizing; fourth, price regulation if necessary.
A stabilized price structure means automatically a stabilized money, and if all the nations agree on a standard at which they will keep their money in step, so to speak, they will voluntarily maintain monetary stabilization.
What this house should now be considering is an effective mechanism for trade stabilization, trade equalization. The terror of all nations to-day is the 'United States. The United States has an appalling productive potential, largely developed since world war I, She towers aloft industrially, a colossal giant among the nations. She stamps about among the other nations literally a Hercules among pygmies.
The generous, noble, idealistic people of the United States do not realize their strength, do not recognize their weight, do not apprehend the fearful damage a careless move on their part can do. The people of the United States therefore do not appreciate their limitless responsibility in these times. Britain is fully aware of these things. Britain has been manoeuvring desperately to escape destruction. Lmited States officials meanwhile have been endeavouring to club Britain into accepting Bretton Woods, and the mere fact that Britain has stood out so long and so earnestly against Bretton Woods ought to be evidence that she realizes that it is certainly to her great detriment. But United States officials have at last bludgeoned and threatened to starve her into accepting the Bretton Woods proposals.
What should Canada's part now be? To take up a club and help the United States to demolish Britain, or sound the alarm, parry the blows, reason with the United States, and try to restrain her recklessness? The social credit movement is sounding the alarm. The supporters of Bretton Woods will argue: Surely the United States would never have accepted Bretton Woods merely to please a handful of holders of gold. There must have been other reasons." Well, there were. The United States political leaders dread unemployment. They have been told that' they are likely to have twenty million unemployed shortly after returning to normal. They see the possibility of dealing with this threat of unemployment only by selling abroad. Bretton Woods would break down the defences against American goods, against American investments, 
against American economic warfare, against American industrial imperialism. Therefore American politicians favour Bretton Woods. American politicians see in Bretton Woods an instrument to help the United States to export her unemployment and dump it in the luckless laps of her neighbours all over the world, no matter where or what the loss to those neighbours so long as the United States can rid herself of her problem of unemployment.
American manufacturers, too, like Bretton Woods. They see too little purchasing power among post-war Americans to buy American goods. They see too few markets. Like Canadians, they stubbornly refuse to adopt a financial system like social credit that would distribute American goods abundantly among American people, a system like social credit that would distribute American goods abroad in such a way as would help and not hinder the people concerned. They will support, therefore, a Bretton Woods to help Americans cram their goods down the world's neck, regardless of whether the world lives or dies. Yes, American industrial imperialists also favour Bretton Woods.
American rich men also support Bretton Woods. They would like to lend abroad. They would fear to lend lest they lose their money as they did in the roaring twenties. The Bretton Woods bank will lend to the poorer nations loans that might be lost. Behind the Bretton Woods bank Americans would rope in forty-three sucker nations to help absorb the losses. Then American rich men can lend to safer risks, loans that cannot be repaid, because the United States will not admit goods that will repay them.' Attractive prospect, is it not? Attractive for all but the victims. Yes, informed American rich men support Bretton Woods.
Anti-British Americans also would back Bretton Woods; those numerous millions of Americans pandered to by the Hearst publications; -those Americans who take delight in twisting the British lion's tail; those Americans who fail to appraise correctly the sacrifice of British heroism that guarded the United States in the deep, dark days of war; those Americans who fail to perceive in Britain and in the British nations the greatest guarantee of human security and freedom through the years that yet must be.
Yes, anti-British Americans also back Bretton Woods. Considering all these matters, Mr. Speaker, it is easy to see why the United States adopted Bretton Woods. Considering these same matters, it ought to be easy to see why Canada ought to reject Bretton Woods.

Bretton Woods Agreements
I have spoken plainly about the United States in relation to Bretton Woods. Plain speaking is by no means an indication of any unkindliness in me toward the United States. We are living in fateful times. Men must uncover the facts affecting one another. United States people have always been shrewd bargainers. They should take no offence if their neighbours indulge in a little critical thinking and speaking, too.
I value United States friendship. I appreciate the help she has given us through the years. I desire that British and Americans continue to be friends. To do so we must understand each other. Most Americans have no desire to hurt the British or any one else. All they wish is to help themselves. They would expect us to look after our own interests. We should be weak, if not recreant in our duty, if we permitted the Americans unwittingly to destroy their best friends. Destroying the British commonwealth they would be setting the stage for their own destruction.
Notwithstanding all the disadvantages to which I have referred, we might regard Bretton Woods with some favour if it provided any means whereby to solve the present economic problems of the world; or if it offered any worthwhile advantage to Canada. But Bretton Woods contains no hint of such a solution, no suggestion of any worthwhile advantage.
The promoters of Bretton Woods will challenge my remarks. I stand ready to prove to the hilt what I have said on the floor of this house and before the members of this house in open committee. The economic problems of the world all stem from adverse trade balances, or the fear of adverse trade balances. Adverse trade balances result in unrepayable debt, in economic conquest and ultimate eeon-A omic devastation and ruin. To guard against such disasters nations resort to protective tariffs, to exchange control, to quotas, to devaluation of currency, currency irregularities, and other irregularities which Bretton Woods is supposed to be designed to prevent or to overcome. These so-called trade restrictions are mainly, if not wholly, protective devices to ward off annihilation. In all its clauses Bretton Woods contains not one phrase suggesting how adverse trade balances can be avoided, not one stipulation that might protect weaker countries from ruinous price competition of stronger economies, not one regulation requiring stronger economies to accept goods in repayment of debts, even debts unavoidably incurred through inability to resist aggressive competition.
Bretton Woods gives all its advantages to creditor nations, those that require no advantages. To the weaker nations it offers no
appreciable help-only hindrance. Follow through Bretton Woods, read it for yourselves, you will find all the things that I have said amply justified and supported there. I and my group will point them out. It leaves the world's economic problems exactly where it found them, except that it aggravates them. Meanwhile it proposes to put the nations in a financial strait-jacket, impairing what little freedom they might have to help themselves. I know that this afternoon the minister said that it did not put the nations in a strait-jacket. We are going to give the minister ample opportunity to prove what he said before we finish this debate. .
Bretton Woods is not a happy compromise. It is the total maintenance of United States economic bargaining power coupled with complete renunciation of bargaining power of the debtor nations. It will therefore benefit only the United States, and perhaps Canada to the extent to which Canada becomes a creditor nation.
Upon the members of the house, upon the people of Canada, upon all British peoples everywhere I urge the warning:	Beware -the
menace of Bretton Woods.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this Bretton Woods agreement which grew out of a conference there in New Hampshire in July last. It was not a treaty; it was a conference held at what is known as Bretton Woods. The proposal is to establish by an agreement first an international monetary fund, and second an international bank for reconstruction and development. It is a charge of over $700 million on the consolidated revenue fund of this country over the head of parliament.
These are very grave times financially for the people of Canada. I am not opposed to an international monetary mechanism being established to solve the economic conditions which are growing out of the war, but I am opposed to the present proposals and I propose to show the reasons why and give the view of two great British chancellors of the exchequer, Sir Kingsley-Wood, who died during the war, and Sir John Anderson, a brilliant administrator of many public departments in the old land before and during the war. If I mistake not, he was here the other day and sat with the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) the day Mr. Attlee and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) were here. This was not, by the widest stretch of the imagination, a conference of forty-four governments. It was held at a place called Bretton Woods, away up in New Hampshire; and when history is written fifty years from now it
Bretton Woods Agreements

will refer to the babes in. the woods who formulated this proposal, because as I say, in the end it will mean the dissolution of the British empire. We are at a critical period in the history of this country and the history of the British empire. I have referred already to the extent to which the mother country suffered during the war, in common with the dominions and the whole civilized world. We had a similar proposal at Dumbarton Oaks and a new united nations policy made at San Francisco, at a conference of the same forty-four bodies which grew up together. Now they have moved on to London, England, and we shall see what happens there. At Bretton Woods there was a large delegation from Brazil; there were delegations from many other countries, but they overlooked one thing. They did not have Sousa's band with them when this agreement was being discussed away up in the woods. In the olden days hardly a public meeting was held at which on all national occasions a brass band or a fife and drum band did not put in an appearance. Sometimes we see these bands on March 17, sometimes on that other great national holiday, July 12.
I want to point out the great objection to these proposals. This was an original idea which Lord Keynes got about 1942 or 1943. He thought he could get up an international financial mechanism that would cure all the financial mistakes from which the world is suffering. Mind you, there is a very large body of public opinion in England which believes in some of the policies which hon. gentlemen to my left have supported in this house for some time. What I have to say will be in part quoted and taken very largely from a British white paper and a white paper issued in the United States, together with a few quotations from a great British financier, Mr. Richard Boothby, who has been a great economic leader in England, following the work of this and other world affairs, and who was one of the advisers to the late Churchill government, with comments of my own, on the whole agreement and the errors I see in it.
These are not at all new proposals; they have been made after other wars. Like the proposals for collective security, they have' been made from the time of Philip of Spain, Louis XIV and Napoleon, and we have heard them twice in our generation. The agreement seeks to set up an international monetary fund. Look at some of the things that have been done in the past under these international proposals. Do not forget the league of nations, Locarno, the Young plan, the Kellogg notes, the Dawes plan, and all the rest of it. Do not forget those who supported all such

agreements and, when war came, were not prepared to let off even a fire-cracker or a sky-rocket to support those who were prepared to back up the allied cause. Now it is proposed that we enter upon another financial policy that is going to cost $700,000,000. Well, as I said to my hon. friend the master of ceremonies, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) the other night, when you get up into the clouds do not forget and old Scot proverb, to keep one foot on the earth. I believe the Minister of Finance would do well to heed that good Scots advice in connection with these proposals and the astronomical altitude of these figures.
As I said, this was not a conference of forty-four nations at all; it was a conference of what I would call economists. Well, the woods are full of economists. I come from Toronto, and lately I have seen more economists than ever before in my life; economists high and low, rich and poor. They have brought forward many proposals; I remember them all when I had to float bonds for $100,000.000 in connection with public utilities in our city. We hear of many financial war proposals, but when they are weighed in the balance most of them are found wanting. What did they do down at this great place called Bretton Woods? Oh, there were great financial plans and carryings on in the woods in old New Hampshire. I saw pictures of these delegates in the Saturday Evening Post, in Lije and in many other magazines, showing views of the representatives of these forty-four nations who were having the time of their lives there. Now here we are to-night, going over the heads of the people of this country and putting on a mortgage of $700,000,000 to be paid out of the consolidated revenues of this country on such a half-baked scheme. Why, we are not only going to bankrupt Canada; if this proposal goes through it will mean the liquidation of the British empire and cause dearer money, and I say that without fear of contradiction. I call to my support statements appearing in the British Hansard by members in the debate of 1943 and in the records of the senate and congress at Washington.
At Fort Knox in the United States they have all the gold in the world piled up. I saw a picture of it in a magazine. Why, the pyramids of Egypt are not to be compared in magnitude or astronomical height with the gold piled up there! That is a celebrated fort and a celebrated state, from which a great general came during the war between the north and south. You know, Mr. Speaker, this proposal reminds me of a scene from Pinafore, with act I, act II and the final act

Bretton Woods Agreements
now before us. Act I is the preliminary, to get the actors ready. I remember the non. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) in private theatricals. When I was interlocutor at a minstrel show I could ask my end-man some questions. Then in this agreement they have the final act; they are going to ring down the curtain. That final act is to be performed to-night; we are to vote $700 million. Why, it gives me a headache even to think of that much money. If we have a few cents in our pockets we are very lucky. I see more gold on some of the uniforms walking up Sparks street than some Canadians ever had in their pockets. But the final act is not really the final act at all, because the proposals of Lord Keynes are not applied.
At this conference they had delegations from Bolivia, Brazil and, in fact, from all over the world. I have not heard the names of some of these countries since I studied geography in school, and I cannot pronounce them all now. No doubt these were all good people, but when you get down to brass tacks, how many of these countries are going to put any cash into the bank? Remember these countries who were in default to the league of nations. Do not forget the man who* broke the bank at Monte Carlo. He was just as good a financier as some of those dealing with this problem, and I would have as much confidence in him as a financier. The final act on the white paper now before us of these experts is one of the most confused articles I have ever read. It contradicts itself; it is obscure; and as a state paper it will cause historians to wonder what kind of parliaments we had here and in all the other forty-four countries, to pass a half-baked scheme like this under which Canada is to put up S700 million. Canada, though, is to put up $700 million. The Tupper government which in my opinion, was a very good government-and I am entitled to my opinion, the same as the educated hon. gentlemen to my left and to my right-required only $36 million to rim this whole country in 1896. But here this evening in one vote before the House of Commons, with no bill and only a resolution, we are faced with an expenditure of $700 million out of the consolidated revenue fund. If we go on piling up that kind of debts and capitalization on our consolidated revenue fund, not only will the country be bankrupt, but the banks will be bankrupt, and the so-called international monetary bank that is being proposed will not be successful.
Mr. Morgenthau, the former secretary of the treasury, is one of the very able gentlemen in Washington. He has said that San Francisco, Dumbarton Oaks and Bretton Woods are
all interrelated. So they are. Even so, I fail to see how they are going to solve the questions of international debt, international credit and international reconstruction after the war. They are not going to be able to solve by the Bretton Woods agreement the building up of the devastated countries of Europe, and countries throughout the world. I fail to see it.
Then, I should like to say a word or two about another matter. First of all, we are going to get back to the gold standard at exchange rates fixed at the level between March and November 1945. That is what the white paper says. We are not allowed to go off it again. They devalue our currency up to ten per cent-a most doubtful expedient under modern conditions. Under the old gold standard you could lose gold once and for all, and, if necessary, suspend payments by a simple decision of the government. Under the proposed gold standard we have to win back the gold equivalent that we may lose over two or three years in order to avoid charges which can apparently be fixed at the discretion of the fund. The implication is that these charges would be made penal.
If we do not do what we are told under this international authority there is power to enforce penalties and sanctions, if deemed necessary, against the people of Canada for a charge in one year amounting to $700 million, and all this for the benefit of some of the Latin republics to the south, and other peoples of forty other countries in the civilized world, some of whom may be in default themselves, as some were in payments to the old league of nations, while Canada always, paid up.
I see a banker right before me in the house, and I venture to say that if I walked into his bank I would not get money on such credit as that. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) is a banker, and I doubt if he would lend me a dollar on that kind of credit, based on such security. I can tell you this, that if you get money into some of the banks it is extremely hard to get it out. I know that.
If we do not do what this international authority tells. us to do under the Bretton Woods agreement, we are to be penalized, and sanctions will be enforced against us. We will remember the sanctions passed against Ethiopia on similar occasions. We will recall that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) rose in his place and spoke in favour of imposing sanctions against Ethiopia. If sanctions were imposed the government would have had, by the covenant of the league to send an expeditionary force. That was the position
Bretton Woods Agreements

taken by us at the league of nations. But did they send a force? No, they did not. A respected minister, and a lovable man, the late Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe, rose in his place and repealed all those sanctions. They were tossed out to the four winds of heaven. That was the kind of sanctions they applied, and all within forty-four hours, or forty-eight hours, I believe it was. I have not very much respect for such penalties and sanctions. This is just like those of the old league of nations when imposed.
Let us face the fact that, until the main lines of commercial policy and of reconstruction policy have been settled, it is idle even td discuss an international currency scheme. Our declared economic objectives- stable prices, full employment and cheap money-are not at present those of the Untied States. .There is bound, therefore, to be a sharp divergence of view as to what constitutes a fundamental disequilibrium.
The issues at stake are of immense importance. In 1929 do not forget Britain and we in Canada to a lesser extent were dragged to the depth of an unparalleled economic depression, simply because Britain was tied to a gold standard and therefore to Wall street. It could happen again; it will happen again, if Bretton Woods goes through. As another plan to Bretton Woods, we, through the development and consolidation of the sterling area within the empire and in western Europe, coud build up an economic unit policy, and the achievement of full employment and a rising standard of living within the empire ourselves. Any such project would be killed finally by Bretton Woods.
There was an article recently in the London Times, which stated the following:
The problem before Britain, and the world, cannot be that of a return to the status quo ante 1939, 1929 or even 1914. It is the establishment of a world economic system which, in the completely altered situation of 1944 and 1950 or 1960 can help mankind to move step by step toward the goal of rising standards of well-being and productivity which a generation twice plunged into catastrophe is resolved to achieve.
By that standard Bretton Woods must be judged. By that standard it falls. The final act of Bretton Woods invites us to throw away the only real asset Great Britain and Canada possess in the post-war world, namely the purchasing power of our own home market. That is a most important matter. Whatever else may happen, as Mr. Robert Boothby has so ably said, the Americans are not going to balance exports with imports. When all is said and done no country will depart hurriedly from that position, where it

is forced to place a most substantial measure of control on its own productive capacity in order to have international trade.
Is Great Britain going to import goods with no plan, indiscriminately in the hope that somehow7 or other she will get enough gold to pay for them, or is she going to use her purchasing power and productive capacity to ensure that she gets imports which she needs?
Is she going to subordinate the maintenance of employment and of essential services to a half-baked international currency scheme which will never work. Is Great Britain going to import goods freely with no plan and just trust to luck, and pay for them in the manner indicated? , I say no. Is she going to permit the maintenance of imports to carry out that scheme? No.
Then, another point arises in connection with bilateral trade agrerements. Some hon. members w7ill recall when Canada had preferential trade agreements some years ago. A treaty was made about twenty years ago with some thirty countries, I believe it was. All that will be extinguished if this goes through. The bilateral trade agreements w7ill be extinct.
In the future they w7ill be turned into regional agreements.
There are many other aspects of this agreement, Mr. Robert Boothby says, "that cause anxiety." I will mention only one:
The proposed agreement, if implemented, would result after a transition period of doubtful length in curtailing the existing convertibility of sterling within the sterling area. This must lead to the complete blocking of all existing sterling balances and, therefore, to the end of the sterling area which is to-day the main source of our economic strength. Here we leave the realm of pure economics for that of politics.	i
What is the long-term policy of Great Britain to be under this proposed Bretton Woods agreement? What is to be the longterm policy of the United States? We have been trying to learn what is to be the longterm policy of Canada. We have been trying to learn what the policy of this country is in connection with our relations within the empire. What is the long-term policy of Canada in connection with this agreement? Seven hundred million dollars will have to be raised, partly out of income, partly out of capital and partly from the sale of bonds. If the people of this country had known about this agreement three weeks ago it would have affected the sale of victory bonds throughout Canada.
Seven hundred million dollars is to be paid out under this agreement which like the Locarno treaty, the Kellogg pact, the Ethiopian sanctions, the Young and Dawes plans,

Bretton Woods Agreements
the league, the finance league and all the rest of them, will turn out to be nothing more than a scrap of paper after we pay in our money, if default comes. That is all we are getting under this one. They have not considered Canada's long-term policy in connection with this agreement. What are they doing by this agreement? There is an absence, as the author I quoted says, "of any directives to the Bretton Woods conference which results in the general muddle and confusion in which we now find ourselves. Are we going to get back to the economic system of the nineteenth century? Is free multilateral trade, laissez-faire and a free convertible international currency based on gold the ultimate or the most desirable objective? That system presupposed five conditions; an expanding world population, expanding frontiers, the free 'migration of human beings, a continuous reduction of tariff barriers and continuous fresh discoveries of gold. None of these exist to-day."
The British can be pretty sure that whatever else they may do the United States are not going to balance exports with imports, reduce tariffs or control the export of gold. Oh, no' after all this they will erect the highest tariff wall in the world. Devaluation is no substitute for import control. What we want is the assurance of a sufficiency of imports of raw materials to maintain our available factors of production at a high level of activity.
In conclusion, I should like to refer to what was said by the late Sir Kingsley-Wood, former chancellor of the exchequer. I intend to quote from a white paper published by the British government. Sir Kingsley-Wood said, speaking in the British House of Commons in 1943, on his budget:
We need a policy of expansion so that employment is maintained and production serves the. ends of consumption.
He went on to give the reasons for that policy. Two plans were proposed. The first was the British plan; the second was the United States plan and they had a head-on collision at Bretton Woods. That was the last of the two plans. The British plan was contained in a document entitled "Proposals for an international clearing union." This international clearing union was to be based on international bank money which would be accepted by all member states for the purposes of payments arising out of international trade. Lord Keynes was closely identified with this scheme for an international clearing union. The government decided to publish this document as a preliminary contribution to the solution of one of the problems of economic cooperation after the war. The 47696-193
government stated that any proposals for a satisfactory international monetary mechanism after the war could be framed only after full consideration of all aspects of a difficult problem.
What about the United States plan? The United States document was entitled "United States proposal for a united and associated nations stabilization fund." The plan, which was closely associated with Mr. Morgenthau, secretary of the United States treasury department, and Mr. White, an assistant secretary, aimed at establishing an international stabilization fund made up of contributions from member countries. The fund would act as a clearing house for international trade movements carrying out the functions in exchange management of the member nations, with all their accumulated knowledge and resources. Like the British document, the United States proposals were not an expression of the official views of the United States government. The introduction to the document emphasized that the proposals were in every sense tentative, intended as a basis for discussion and exchange of views.
A debate on post-war international currency took place in the British House of Commons on May 12, 1943, and the late Sir Kingsley-Wood, who opened the debate, defined as follows the three aims of the policy; First, to provide a mechanism by which international balances should be freely settled; second, to provide that national exchanges should be reasonably stable, so that goods and services can be marketed with knowledge of the value they command; third, to provide that countries, whose economy has been gravely dislocated or damaged by the war, should have some temporary international monetary facilities to enable them to start trading without undue delay.
The united nations monetary and financial conference was held at Bretton Woods between July 1 and July 22, 1944. Forty-three nations, including Great Britain, attended the conference. The proposals are before the house. The minister explained them to-day. He described the international monetary fund and the international bank for reconstruction and development. Both those proposals were recommended to congress in a message by the late President of the United States.
Sir John Anderson, chancellor of the exchequer, in the budget debate and white paper dealt in some detail with the proposals

Bretton Woods Agreements

put forward at Bretton Woods. He was a great chancellor with the background he had. He said with regard to Bretton Woods:
The Bretton Woods doeumeftt explicitly recognized that while we might agree on objectives and methods when the world's trade was settling down, countries like our own had to face an extremely difficult period of transition in which they must keep their hands free to deal with their difficulties as they arose.
There is one point that I must brinj* to the attention of some of the critics of the final act. I mean those who appear to think that the line of safety for us after the war is to reserve our full rights to enter into discriminatory commercial and currency agreements, not only as a temporary measure during the transitional period, but permanently.
And again:
Under article VII of the Mutual Aid_ agreement, the master agreement under which we have received assistance of prodigious amount, we agreed to work for the elimination of all forms of discrimination in international commerce. The only qualification was concerned with imperial preferences. We are bound by this agreement and we are going to honour it..
Good. That last word is my own. I continue :
Quite apart from the Mutual Aid agreement, by our commercial agreement with the United States of 1938 we also accepted a policy of nondiscrimination in trade. I would ask those who recommend what is in essence a barter system as the basis for our international trade; do they really wish us to follow a course which goes back on what we have agreed with the United States and flouts one of the principles of international commerce to which the United States government attach importance, and which, as a matter of fact, I believe in our own interest is a sound principle? If we discriminate, other people can discriminate. If we indulge in barter, other people can indulge in barter.	,
I am also told that the Bretton Woods conference means a return to the gold standard. I doubt -whether those critics who use the words "gold standard" as a term of opprobrium always have a perfectly clear idea of what they mean, but perhaps one can assume that what they are thinking of is a system under which the external value of sterling was fixed, and the internal credit policy was made subservient to the maintenance of that value. To that system, if it ever existed in such a crude form, we do not propose to return.
The Lord Chancellor refers in conclusion to the problem of stability of exchange rates:
I do not go the whole way in believing that the greater part of our troubles between the wars was caused by unstable exchanges. Nor do I believe that countries with a major interest in international trade lightly alter their exchange rates. Those alterations disturb internal as well as external values. But there is no doubt that the instability of the exchange rates of some important countries at some periods between the wars was a disturbing factor in international trade.

His conclusions are expressed in the following two paragraphs:
The Bretton Woods document follows a middle course in this matter. So far from imposing a system of rigid exchange rates, it expressly recognizes the need for adjustment of exchange rates to correct disequilibrium. If we believe it is in our own interests to have a reasonable stability of exchanges but at the same time to have a method for the orderly .adjustment of exchanges when the occasion arises, I do not see very well how one could have a very different principle from that stated in the Bretton Woods document.
It is, of course, true that to a certain extent we would bring our exchange policy under review by an international body on which we 'should be represented. But so would every other country. We would not surrender any ultimate right to follow our own policy, but we would accept an obligation to recognize that the adjustment of the exchange value of sterling, or of any other major international currency, is a two-ended process, and that we owe it to the general interests of international trade to consult with an international institution before _we make a change which will affect our commercial, as well as our financial, relations with other countries.
Those are the views 'of two British chancellors of the exchequer.
My opinion, Mr. Speaker, is that the time has not arrived for such a proposal. We should deal as our first task with the great questions of trade, defence, migration, and preferential trade within the empire. I will contend first, last and all the time that the primary matter for us to- consider and predicate in any agreement that we sign in this connection is, that we shall stay within the British empire. That empire, functioning along the lines I indicated to-day, is strong enough to stand any strain or stress of war, peace or reconstruction.
I say further, in conclusion, that it will be far better to make agreements with our own dominions along the lines of the united nations council; we should then have an empire council of the same general character as the united nations organization and decide first our own empire policies. Unless we do that the states of the empire will be divided and broken up, for if the dominions do not hang together they will hang separately. Together they are the strongest in the whole world and self-contained in a financial, material way and in a constitutional, social and economic way, to withstand the world.
Where do we in Canada stand? We have heard a great deal to-day about international policies, and this apparently is one of them. They are much in favour with some hon. gentlemen. But where do we stand at this critical hour in relation to the British empire? If we are to proceed far along these separatist lines we shall, I fear, lead to the dissolution

of the British empire in a period of time. This Bretton Woods agreement will, in my opinion, lead to restricted trade and dearer money, and also, as Mr. Churchill has said, "to the dissolution of the British empire".

I believe this is one of the most important and dangerous measures ever to be submitted to this House of Commons. In all seriousness I say -that I look upon this measure as being an act of treachery not only to the British commonwealth of nations but to every peace-loving nation in the world to-day.
A short tim'e ago we endorsed in this house a charter for the united nations, the main purpose of which was to maintain international peace and security, to develop friendly relationships among nations, and to encourage respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. If the measure now before us passes, I believe that wje shall be making a mockery of the charter, because you cannot make political agreements to maintain peace at the same time that you institute economic agreements to declare a form of international trade war. The result, I -think all hon. members will agree, must be international friction which will greatly menace the success of any charter of peace. Therefore, if the final act of the Bretton Woods conference is to be regarded as the cornerstone of intera-tional economic cooperation, it is essential that it receive the most careful consideration by all hon. members of this house. I am well aware that there are those who will argue that this measure has already received the careful attention of Canadian experts, and that these men are far better qualified to judge of the merits or demerits of this measure than we are. Well, as I have remarked before in this chamber, I judge a man by his record; and the record of these men is not an impressive one.

the army because they w^re medically unfit, due very largely to malnutrition. I would ask, is that a record to inspire confidence?
Furthermore, their war record is no better. We have heard a number of people praise the financial record of the government in the war, but is it one which will bear close scrutiny? I recall that in 1939 the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) stated that the wrar financial policy of the government was to be as far as possible a pay-as-you-go policy; and yet what has happened? We consider that a thorough explanation of these proposals should be given to the house before second reading, because on second reading you endorse the principle. The minister has no right to ask the members of this house to endorse -the principle of a measure which he himself admits is very complex and hard to understand. I doubt whether more than two or three per cent of the members of this house understand it; I would put the percentage even lower, because I doubt very much if even the experts themselves understand it. I think this is quite evident when one finds that men like Maynard Keynes and Morgenthau disagree as to exactly what the act means. In England the people are told that it is not the gold standard; yet in the United States it is represented as the fruition of the treasury's gold policy.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The late President of the United States, Franklin D. Roosevelt, sent a message to be read before the senate on February 12, 1945, relating to the Bretton Woods agreement. It read in part as follows:
If we are to measure up to the task of peace with the same stature as we have measured up -to the task of war, we must see that the institutions of peace rest firmly on the solid foundations of international political -and economic cooperation. The cornerstone for international political cooperation is the Dumbarton Oaks proposal for a permanent united nations. International political relations will be friendly and constructive, however, only if solutions -are found to the difficult economic problems we face to-day. The cornerstone for international economic cooperation is the Bretton Woods -proposal for an international monetary fund and an international bank for reconstruction and development.
Bretton Woods Agreements

That is just about the same thing that the minister said when he was introducing the motion before the house. Therefore, if the agreement is to be part of the foundation upon which we hope to build world peace, it must be of such a nature 'as to promote friendship and good will among the nations of the world, and it is upon that basis that I intend to discuss the final act this evening. Is the Bretton Woods act likely to help to promote good will among the members? If not, I believe that all members of this Bouse will agree that it should be discarded. In article I, the purposes of the act are defined, and I should like to read the purposes of the international fund, section 1:
(i)	To promote international monetary cooperation through a permanent institution which provides the machinery for consultation and collaboration on international monetary problems.
(ii)	To facilitate the expansion and balanced growth of international trade, and to contribute
' thereby to the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real income and to the development of the productive resources of all members as primary objectives of economic policy.
All members will agree with the purposes outlined in sections 1 and 2. I wish to comment upon 3, 4 and 5:
(iii)	To promote exchange stability, to maintain orderly exchange arrangements among members, and to avoid competitive exchange depreciation.
(iv)	To assist in the establishment of a multilateral system of payments in respect of current transactions between members and in the elimination of foreign' exchange restrictions which hamper the growth of world trade.
(v)	To give confidence to members by making the fund's resources available to them under adequate safeguards, thus providing them with opportunity to correct maladjustments in their balance of payments without resorting to measures destructive of national or international prosperity.
The questions that must come to the minds of hon. members are these: Why do nations indulge in exchange depreciation? Why do nations impose foreign exchange restrictions? Why is there unbalance of trade between nations when both parties are endeavouring to export goods? I would say that we must have the answers to these questions before we can judge of the adequacy of the proposals in this act.
Article I, section II, states that the purpose of the fund is to facilitate the expansion and balanced growth of international trade. Unfortunately, the fund concentrates on bringing about a balance of money between nations, with all the emphasis on gold and on United States dollars, ignoring the fact that in the long run you cannot have a bal-
	.
ance of money without a balance of trade, except of course by the steady growth of debt between nations, and that is provided for in article 7 of the act. I will quote section 2 of article 7:
The fund may, if it deems such action appropriate to replenish its holdings of any member's currency, take either or both of the following steps:
(i)	Propose to the member that, on terms and conditions agreed between the fund and the member, the latter lend its currency to the fund or that, with the approval of the member, the fund borrow such currency from some other source either within or outside the territories of the member, but no member shall he under any obigation to make such loans to the fund or to approve the borrowing of its currency by the fund from any other source.
(ii)	Require the member to sell its currency to the fund for gold.
That is to say, if the United States consistently refuses to accept imports in exchange for its exports, thereby depriving other nations of dollars to pay for imports, then the fund can borrow or buy with [DOT] gold, dollars from the United States to enable the debtor nations to balance their payments. But, mark you, it would be done by going into debt instead of by balancing trade and having an exchange of goods. Therefore one of my main arguments against the fund is that, in attempting to bring about balance of payments, instead of ensuring that it shall be done through a balance of trade it attains its object by expanding the debt of the debtor nation.
Let me ask hon. members this question: 'Is that a sound basis upon which to attempt to promote friendship and good will among the nations of the world, by forcing a nation to go into debt in order to obtain the goods it requires when it has goods on hand which it is willing to exchange? The express purpose of the fund is to facilitate the expansion and balanced growth of international trade. Then what is the main or real purpose of international trade?
Every time I hear the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) speak, I get the impression that the main purpose of trade is to export goods. I have never once heard him emphasize at the same time the even greater importance of importing goods in return. Does anyone really think that a nation can become prosperous by exporting goods? You merely remove goods from the nation and lower the standard of living to that extent, so that export trade by itself cannot bring prosperity unless exports are used for the purpose of bringing imports back into the country.

Breltnn Woods Agreements
And so, reducing international trade to its simplest terms, we say that it is the exchange of those goods which we cannot consume for those goods which we cannot produce, thereby bringing about an improvement in the people's standard of living. It should be an act of mutual advantage to the parties concerned. Therefore to the extent that you expand foreign trade on that basis you improve the nation's standard of living. But when you maintain your foreign trade on the basis of trying to maintain a favourable balance of trade you are lowering the standard of living of the people to that extent. Unfortunately that has been the basis for foreign trade in the past.
Highly industralized nations have endeavoured to export more than they were prepared to take back in imports, thereby lowering the standard of living, the reason being the lack of buying power internally and not because the people do not need the goods.
I wish to quote from a statement made by Reginald McKenna to the banker's association, on October 5, 1922. I have quoted it on previous occasions, but it has a direct bearing on this question and therefore I should like to quote it again at this time:
For over two centuries, British capital, that is, credit had been lent to other countries, year by year England produced more than she either consumed herself or could exchange for the products of other nations, and she could not obtain a market for the surplus unless she gave the purchaser & long credit. Foreign loans and ioreign issues were taken up in England and the proceeds were spent in paying for surplus production. British factories land workshops were kept in good employment, but it was a condition of their -prosperity that a part of their output should be disposed of in this way.
Note that, according to Reginald McKenna, the prosperity of England depended upon her being able to sell more goods abroad than she brought back in return. In other words, that was the old idea that a favourable balance of trade maintained prosperity. But what did it really mean. It meant that owing to the deficiency of purchasing power that existed in England, and by maintaining a favourable balance of trade, the wages that were paid out in the production of those goods which were exported and for which no imports were brought back in return helped to create a demand for the goods that were left within the country and, as McKenna stated, it maintained a certain degree of prosperity in England. I would not say that it maintained prosperity for the people of England. Nobody who knew conditions in England in those years would suggest that all people were prosperous, but it did maintain prosperity for the industrialists.
It is true that it served the industrialists and the manufacturers of England well during the two centuries prior to the last war. What happened in the later years? Shortly before the last war other nations were also starting to become industrialized and to raise tariffs to keep British goods out, because they also were finding themselves in a position where it became necessary to maintain a favourable balance of trade in order to maintain employment within their own borders. The year 1914 saw the end of that type of policy. I remember in the years 1906, 1907, 1908, 1912 and 1913 watching the marches of the unemployed in the city of London. I say that any nation that attempts in the future to maintain prosperity within its own borders by that policy is bound to fail. Not only will it fail, but it will help to create throughout the world a condition which will bring about unrest, international friction and war.
That was also the policy between the two wars, the war of 1914-18 and the war of 1934-45, with the difference that after 1929 the United States, while giving credit for trade exports, demanded payment not in goods but in gold or foreign securities. We know what the policy was in 1929 and during the thirties. It caused one of the most violent depressions the world has ever seen, because at that time the nations were on the gold standard, and as gold was withdrawn from those countries their gold reserves were reduced and a general restriction of currency took place in all countries.
We find to-day that all highly industrialized nations are prepared for a fight for foreign markets after the war. For example, both Canada and the United States feel that in order to maintain the full development of their resources they will have to make large-scale foreign investments after the conclusion of hostilities.
I hold in my hand a booklet which is an address delivered by Mr. William C. Clark on post-war goals and economic reconstruction at New York university on December 15, 1943. On pages 221 he states:
We feel also that adequate arrangements are essential to make possible a substantial volume of long-term international investment, and we trust that the technical and political difficulties involved in consummating these may soon be surmounted.
