speechtext:
He is the deputy minister
of Finance. Those members who were on the reconstruction committee last year will remember that rvhen we were discussing these monetary stabilization proposals I asked him whether or not he considered foreign investments a long-term solution, and he admitted
Bretton Woods Agreements

that they were not a long-term solution. While 1 feel that at this time we should be prepared to develop policies that would be a long-term solution, on the other hand is there justification for. them even as a short-term solution? Is there any justification at the present time for Canada going into a large scheme of foreign investment. I know we have certain moral obligations, but aside from that I would say there can be no justification for such a policy until we have completed or have well advanced the development of our own country.
I think it is timq that we had a little more investment in roads in this country, especially in western Canada. Why not invest money-in the development of our north country? .Why not invest money in irrigation in western Canada? Why not invest in a real live, wide housing scheme in Canada? Why not make greater investments in the greatest asset of this country, Canadian youth?
Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, public opinion is beginning to realize the fallacy of prosperity by foreign investment. I should like to quote from a speech made on June 7, 1945, by the governor of New York. This is what he said:
We in the United States will emerge from the war with overwhelming power, financial and industrial. There is no question of the huge demand for our exports that will exist. The great question is whether we are prepared to accept payment for these goods in the only sound way that payment can be made-by baking in exchange the goods and services of other nations. The American people have made clear their determination to join with other nations in a world organization to maintain peace; but real peace cannot be achieved merely in the political field. AH of the work being done at San Francisco will mean tragically little if economic conflict is to divide the nation.
The London chamber of commerce, probably one of the greatest organizations of its kind, has emphasized this question time and again. I have quoted it in the house, and therefore I am not going to take the time to quote it again at this moment, but I should like to quote from a statement of the-London Economist because it is generally' considered an orthodox publication. I quote from the London Economist of August 11, 1945, page 182:
The condition of full employment as it is now universally recognized is that the economy should generate a sufficiently large flow of effective demand to purchase the whole of the gross national product. In simpler language, somebody has to buy the volume of goods that full employment will produce, or they will not be produced.
That is to say, if a nation's purchasing power is adjusted so as to enable the people to buy the total production of the nation, or at least all the goods that they desire, then a

nation will be willing to accept imports in return for its exports. So that the, first step toward any sound scheme for international trade is for each "and every nation to set its own house in order and expand the purchasing power of the people to the point where they are able to buy' the total production of the country, or the production of other nations for which their own production can be exchanged. It is futile to hope that any form of international stabilization can maintain international trade on a sound basis until each nation is first of all prepared to set its own house in order. Therefore I would emphasize that the responsibility must rest with the Canadian government to expand the purchasing power of the people of this country to the point where they- are able to buy the total production of the country. I am not going to take the lime to show how that can be done. When speaking the other day, the leader of this group gave a clear way in which this might be brought about. We have referred to it on various occasions, and no doubt will do so in the future. I think the house is familiar with the proposals that we have set forth from time to time by which the purchasing power can be expanded to maintain an effective demand.
Unfortunately it has been customary' in the past to regard the cause of an unbalance of trade as arising from a nation buying more than it can afford or borrowing more than it can repay. Apparently it is only recently we have come to realize that, a creditor may be and very' frequently is to blame, that it arises from a creditor nation attempting to dump its unemployment problem upon the doorstep of another nation by exporting abroad Jar more goods than it is prepared to accept payment for in imports from the world at large on a multilateral basis. Obviously, if some nations insist on exporting more than they are willing to accept in return there are bound to be some nations forced into debt in order to obtain the goods they require, even though they have goods to export in, exchange. In other words, if some nations insist upon maintaining a favourable balance of payments, other nations must find themselves in the unfortunate position of having an unfavourable balance. As a consequence, nations suffering from an unfavourable balance of trade have resorted to currency depreciation and foreign exchange restrictions as necessary protection against being forced into a state of unpayable debt. For example, a nation depreciating its currency by twenty per cent is able to undersell another nation by twenty per cent, and thereby encourage other nations to buy more of their gogds, thereby

Bretton Woods Agreements
hoping to readjust the balance of payments. For the same reason a nation may impose foreign exchange restrictions to prevent the flight of capital, which would lead to still further unbalanced payments. Therefore we feel that before-taking these protective measures away from a nation or even curtailing them, we must take the necessary steps to remove the cause of the unbalance of trade. In other words, we must recognize the responsibility of the creditor nation to accept payment in the only way a debtor nation can make payment, namely in goods and services, unless of course the nation happens to be a producer of gold; and there are very few nations, comparatively speaking, that are producers of gold.
I wish to examine the Bretton Woods agreement in the light of those facts. The act comprises the articles of agreement of the international monetary fund and the international bank for reconstruction and development. I believe hon. members who have studied the act will agree that it is very hard to understand exactly what is meant by the phraseology used. I doubt if a single member of the house to-day, even including the Minister of Finance, would dare say he can explain exactly what every section of this act means. Therefore it is not surprising, as I stated a while ago, that different interpretations have been given by Maynard Keynes and Mr. Morgenthau. I stated in my first words that Mr. Morganthau had said what this meant. In presenting his report to congress on international finance he stated: "The Bretton Woods plan marks the fruition of the American treasury's gold policy," while Mr. Keynes in England stated it did not mean the gold standard at all. Apparently they have different interpretations of the same thing. Certainly I would suggest that any hon. member studying articles IV and V would immediately agree that it is a return to the gold standard. I do not say it is the gold standard of 1925, any more than the gold standard of that year was the same as the gold standard of 1914; but how can anyone argue that it is not the gold standard when these words are used in section 1(a) of article IV:
The par value of the currency of each member shall he expressed in terms of gold as a common denominator or in terms of the United States dollar of the weight and fineness in effect on July 1, 1944.
The leader of the C.C.F. party said in his remarks that he would be opposed to this agreement if it meant that the currency of a nation was to be based upon gold. Here it
definitely states that it is to be based upon gold, and I do not think even an .expert lawyer could wriggle out of that phrase.
To come back to the question of an unbalance of trade, article VII deals with a nation that persists in selling more abroad than it buys. Provision is made for the fund to borrow from the currency of that member nation, provided that the member is agreeable, or the fund may buy its currency for gold which, as I stated before, can only result in the nation having to obtain that currency by means of borrowing and going still further into debt. On the other hand, a very different attitude is taken toward a nation that imports more goods than it is able to pay for with its exports. Section 8 of article V imposes very severe penalties upon a nation finding itself in that awkward predicament. I should like to quote part of that section:
(c)	The fund shall levy charges uniform for all members which shall be payable by any member on the average daily balance of its currency held by the fund in excess of its quota. These charges shall be at the following rates:
(i)	On amounts not more than twenty-five per cent in excess of the quota: no charge for the first three months; one-half per cent per annum for the next nine months: and thereafter an increase in the charge of one-half per cent for each subsequent year.
(ii)	On amounts more than twenty-five per cent and not more than fifty per cent in excess of the quota: an additional one-half per cent for the first year; and an additional one-half per cent for each subsequent year.
(iii)	On each additional bracket of twenty-five per cent in excess of the quota: an additional one-half per cent for the first year; and an additional one-half per cent for each subsequent year.
(d)	Whenever the fund's holdings of a member's currency are such that the charge applicable to any bracket for any period has reached the rate of four per cent per annum, the fund and the member shall consider means by which the fund's holdings of the currency can be reduced. Thereafter the charges shall rise in accordance with the provisions of (c) above until they reach five per cent and failing agreement, the fund may then impose such charges as it deems appropriate.
Imagine any man signing a mortgage under which his interest rates will go up by one-half per cent per annum and then, when they reach a certain amount, if he cannot come to an agreement with the mortgage company the company can charge any rate it likes. Does anyone really think terms of that kind are going to bring about a spirit of good will in this world? The full weight is placed on the debtor nation; no pressure whatever is exerted upon the creditor nation, although to-day we all agree that each nation has a certain responsibility, whether it be a debtor or a creditor nation, in order to maintain an even balance of payment.	.
Bretton Woods Agreements

Time is going, Mr. Speaker, and I wish to shorten my remarks. As I have stated, the inevitable consequence of such a policy will be that, in order to get the goods they require, certain nations, being unable to get other nations to accept their goods in payment', and not being producers of gold, will be forced further and further into a state of unpayable debt, while on the other hand the creditor nations, in order to continue exporting more goods than they are prepared to accept payment for in imports, in order to dump their unemployment problem on the doorstep of another nation, will continue to pile up foreign credits which they will endeavour to use for foreign investments. To-day I think we have a very good example of United States imperialism at its very worst.
So I come back to my original question: can such a policy as the Bretton Woods agreement create a feeling of good will and friendship? I would say that the inevitable consequence must be international friction leading to war. I have often been asked this question: "Why would nations join the fund if the conditions are as you state them to be? They say that nations join on a voluntary basis, and if conditions are as you have mentioned, surely no nation would join." I think it is true that so far only two nations have signed, but the agreement has been signed in behalf of the nations by the experts of some forty-four nations. I would say that the weaker nations joined as a result of economic pressure. I do not think it is fair to say that they have signed on a voluntary basis. They have signed because they have been practically compelled to do so, in order to exist. My suspicion regarding this question was first aroused when resolution No. 12 was first passed at Atlantic City limiting the functions of UNRRA, to all intents and purposes striking out the second "R", and making it a straight relief project, so that no help could be given for reconstruction or rehabilitation. Then, when nations wished to know where they could get help to rebuild industries they were told that they could get it by becoming members or parties to the Bretton Woods agreement.
I was very much struck by an article which appeared in the Fundy Fisherman, of August 29. 1945, which read:
The lend-lease agreements which the various nations were obliged to sign before obtaining supplies contained a provision which was not in the legislation enacted by congress. This laid down that the debtor nations were to enter into agreements directed to the expansion, by appropriate international and domestic measures, of,, production, employment and the exchange and consumption of goods, etc. The international money plan is the first of these measures. It is IMr. Quelch.]
one thing to consider the plan on its merits. It is another matter altogether to discover what the consequence of rejection will be.
I received another article of great interest from The Liberator Council of England, recognized as a monetary reform organization. Sir Charles Morgan-Webb is one of their advisers, a man of world renown as an authority on gold and sterling. This pamphlet, which was circularized among members of parliament in England, states in part:
One of Mr. Winston Churchill's secret and unpublicized actions after assuming power in 1940, was to promise President Roosevelt that he would do all in his power to bring Britain back to a gold standard suitable to American ideas.
I am not criticizing Churchill for that statement, because I realize that England was in a position of life and death in those days. England had to get supplies. And if in order to get. help under lend-lease, as is suggested in the article in the Fundy Fishermen, they had to agree to become a party to the gold standard or Bretton Woods, then no doubt Churchill was justified in giving in to the United States to get the help they required. But I do not think action of that kind redounds to the credit of the United States. It is most interesting to note that, while making an agreement of that kind, Churchill knew very well what the significance of the gold standard would be, because in 1932 he bitterly denounced it. I shall not take time to read his statement. They have been quoted in the house on various occasions.
However, I should like to quote the statement made by Mr. Ernest Bevin when he set out the attitude of the British Labour party regarding the Bretton Woods agreement. This is taken from the parliamentary debates for Monday, June 4, 1945, and he said:
One last word about Bretton Woods. I have never been finally convinced about Bretton Woods. I take the line, and my party takes the line that, neither directly nor indirectly, will we again be anchored to gold in any circumstances.
I shall never be a party to any international agreement, which, either as a result of the fluctuation of exchange, speculation or international action of that kind-which is not always of the highest moral standard-would prevent me from insulating the home market from the violent repercussions which will break down the home price Jevel when these wide fluctuations take place on the international price level. However,
I will join with anyone in finding a rational basis for an international price level, properly organized, provided it does not reflect itself in depressing the standard of life on the home market. As yet, neither the chancellor nor Lord Keynes has ever been able to persuade me that there are sufficient safeguards in the Bretton Woods proposals to achieve that object.
That was the attitude of the British Labour party in June, 1945. But, as I say, when sufficient pressure can be forced upon a nation

Bretton Woods Agreements


:

they are likely to renounce their principles. I should like to quote from the London Economist of July 21, 1945, where it speaks about the Bretton Woods agreement:
As a matter of plain economies, there would seem to be a clear balance of argument against the Bretton Woods scheme-that is against the monetary fund.
Mind you, the London Economist is a most orthodox paper. Yet they say there is a clear balance of argument against the Bretton Woods agreement on economic grounds. The article continues:
But as a matter of politics or, if the word is taken to imply something sinister, of amicable relations between governments, there is almost everything 'to be said in its favour. How much economic hazard is a reasonable price for continued generosity and friendship or at the least for avoidance of American disappointment and resentment. It all depends upon the size of the hazard and the intensity of the friendship.
One	might interject, what friendship!
Apparently the price Great Britain has had to pay to get three and a half billion dollars has been the signing of the Bretton Woods agreement-although it has been condemned by the party in power to-day, through Mr. Ernest Bevin.
In closing, I wish to ask this question: Did the Canadian government help the British government to resist coercion in regard to the signing of the Bretton Woods agreement? Is it fair to say* that the Canadian government added its pressure to that of the United States government in order to try to persuade the British government to become a party to the Bretton Woods agreement.? I understand that the Canadian government is one of those governments which to-day are pushing forward the Bretton Woods agreement. In other words, we have merely become the Charlie McCarthy for Uncle Sam.
Some people will argue, "Well, why worry? Even if a nation joins, it can withdraw." That is true. That is mentioned in the act in several places, namely that a nation can withdraw. But what happens to a nation that withdraws? Article XI deals with that and, although I have not time to quote it, I suggest that every member should read it. It would be seen that the article states that if [DOT] a member withdraws and is no longer a member of the organization, other members may be advised to institute a boycott against that nation. Just visualize what would happen if England were forced to withdraw from this fund, and were no longer to be a member, and the rest of the nations in the British empire placed a boycott against Great Britain!
Was I exaggerating when I said that to my mind this act is nothing more or less than an 47696-194
act of treachery against the British commonwealth of nations? What effect will the act have upon a nation's sovereignty? I am not prepared to say that Bretton Woods will to any extent affect the sovereignty of a creditor nation or a nation that is a gold producer. But in the committee stage I shall prove, I think, without shadow of a doubt, that it does destroy the sovereignty of a debtor nation. Just because she will not suffer loss of sovereignty as a result of this act, so long as she can maintain adequate gold reserves, is Canada justified in trying to impose upon other nations a conditon which will mean the destruction of their sovereignty?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the violent language that has been used against this resolution it would seem that one is at some personal danger in supporting it at all. However, I feel that Bretton Woods is a pious hope to establish multilateral trade by the establishment of an international exchange medium.
I Mr. Quelch.]
It hopes to overcome the international monetary chaos which led directly to the restriction of trade which brought about unemployment, despair and eventual dictatorship, and of course war, in the despair decades of the twenties and thirties of this century.
Naturally any agreement of this nature must impose restrictions upon the signatories to the agreement. No matter what agreement you enter into, by the very nature of its being an agreement you agree with certain other people to do certain things. By its very nature there must be certain restrictions. One of the great visions is the hope that the international trade banditry as practised after the last war will be put an end to.
Probably it will be impossible completely to curtail international trade banditry; it will probably be impossible to overcome many of the dark practices in which international trade indulges from time to time, but this at least is a hopeful step in the right direction. During the period following the last war all kinds of methods were used to import goods, to cut prices, to give drawbacks, and to make secret agreements. One instance was in the timber industry. The Soviet Union said that during the year they would meet any price at which importers could buy in any other * country in the world. That is just typical of the practices that went on.
A little later on we had^the sale of South American securities in the United States, securities which in many cases represented no real value. They were sold, not because they were going to purchase real goods or provide real services, but because in many cases the vendors could find a market for the securities. I happened to be in Vienna when the Oster-reich-Credit-Anstalt failed, and that brought about the failure of one bank after another and eventually caused the bank holiday in the United States in 1933. It was all brought about by a desire to export ^nd not import, and the sharp practices which resulted, that were carried on in international trade and the type of trade that was done. The restrictions of imports, high tariffs, blocked currencies, different types of currencies, all had a part in bringing about the eventual complete destruction of international trade at any level or the, eventual cessation of international trade of magnitude at any level. United States banks failed, and thus the richest country in the world found itself with a bank holiday and a real condition of panic.
In his first inaugural address the late President Roosevelt said that the only thing we had to fear was fear, and yet the entire world was in an economic panic. I do not think there is any other word for it. It was in an

Bretton Woods Agreements
economic panic because there was no international regulation. This is at least an attempt to prevent history from repeating itself. As such I think it is a step very much in the right direction.
We had as we know an entirely fictitious value put on the money of European countries. The German mark, the Italian lira and the Russian ruble may have been worth anything, but as exchange media they were virtually valueless. They were used by the governments of the countries in question for unfair practices and international trade banditry. That is the only word I can think of to describe the practices that went on during that time.
We at the present time may fall into the danger of comparing conditions after the last war with conditions now. While history repeats itself, it does not repeat itself exactly; and while there are many similarities between conditions after the last war and conditions after this war, there are sufficient differences, 1 believe, to be worth mentioning and seriously considering at the present time.
The first difference between the aftermath of this war and that of the last war is that after the last war the United States put on one tariff after another; first of all the emergency tariff, then the Fordney-MeCumber tariff, and then the Hawley-Smoot tariff, and they virtually excluded the goods of the world from their country. This was the first really retrogressive step. Then, with the restriction of imports, they followed a course of extreme isolationism. They refused to sign-this is ancient history, everybody knows it-the Versailles treaty, and they declined to join the league of nations and withdrew' completely into isolationism. From then on things went from bad to worse, and little hope remained of world trade.
At the present time conditions are quite different. The United States is no longer the abundant storehouse she- w7as in 1918; she is becoming a "have-not" country; she is beginning to notice her great depletion of raw materials and to be frightened about it. I refer particularly to some of the non-ferrous metals, copper, lead, zinc and manganese. Of these, the United States, at the rate of consumption which prevailed from 1935 to 1938, has between two and thirty years supply; in most cases, much less than thirty years. The United States will find that she must have these metals for her industries; and we in Canada are, in every case excepting manganese, the greatest producer or potential producer, or at any rate our potential is as great as that of any other nation. Therefore, 47696-194J
instead of our being excluded from the United States market as we were after the last war, it is probable that the Americans will need our base metals.
Further, the Americans have now become almost completely deficient in such vital metals as tin, antimony, chrome and nickel. Of course they never did have any nickel, but they had some of the other metals. They must now import these things in order to carry on their industries. It is possible that the natural source of some of these metals will be Canada, and our past desperate need for United States dollars will probably not be as great as it was after the last war. There used to be a saying in the United States, which had an almost world-wide circulation, "export or die". The present condition is very nearly the reverse; it is "import or perish", because, with these great deficiencies, the United States finds she must import not only for her own safety but to run her industries in general. I submit, therefore, that there is a very great difference between the situation after the last war and the situation at the present time.
Another singular fact worth noting in this connection is that at the present time fewer than two million Americans are working in industries protected by a tariff. We used to think that all United States industry had tariff protection, and during the Hawley-Smoot era most of it had. But now-I will quote my authority for this in a minute-there are fewer than two million Americans w'ho are working in tariff-protected industries, which is a significant figure. So that I think we can discount the theory that this agreement of Bretton Woods is some scheme by which the United States hopes to "put a fast one over" the rest of the world. I do not believe that that is so; in fact I am certain that it is not so. I wish to quote one paragraph from an article from Percy W. Bidwell about the United States deficiency at the present time. It appears in the current issue of "Foreign Affairs" at page 98:	,
Americans will not die, nor Will the United States cease to exist, if we fail to increase our imports. But we shall not live as well as we mighty nor as safely. This is a rich country. The high productivity of our industry gives us abundant supplies of purchasing power in foreign markets.- Unlike Britain, we are under no pressure to restrict imports in order to bring our international accounts into balance. On the contrary, we cannot hope to balance them without expanding our purchases abroad. Yet, with all our riches, we have persisted in playing the miser, spending in normal years less than one per cent of our national income on consumers' goods of foreign manufacture. Instead of reaching out for the useful, appetizing and beautiful things which foreigners are so eager to supply,

Bretton Woods Agreements
we put up tariff walls to protect ourselves against prosperity and abundance. If we will adopt a new attitude toward imports, if we will accept them and make the most of them, we shall increase national security, we shall provide the competitive stimulus necessary to maintain our free-enterprise system at a high pitch of efficiency, and we shall enable our people to attain the high cultural standards befitting a rich and powerful nation.
I do not think that policy sounds as if this Bretton Woods agreement was a sinister United States scheme to restrict imports. They are beginning to realize that they have to "import or die".
Let us now look at the peculiar position of Canada. Canada, as has been so frequently said, was during the war and is at the present time probably the greatest per capita producer of goods for export. I have not the statistics before me, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong; but in normal times, on a per capita basis, Canada was the greatest exporter in the world, with the possible exception of some smaller countries which had greater agricultural exports. I am referring to our exports among manufacturing countries. There were smaller countries that had greater agricultural exports.

speechtext: Such as New Zealand.

speechtext:
Yes. But-and this is a very singular fact-Canada is also a great , exporter of capital. Canadian enterprises supported by Canadian capital are world wide.
I need mention only one or two. The International Petroleum company, while its capital is largely American, is nevertheless a Canadian company with a good deal of Canadian capital, and the Brazilian Traction company is another concern I might mention. It is probably the largest single unit among public utilities in the world. All through South America you will find Canadian capital. You will also find that not only does Canada export capital; she is an exporter of services. Take her trans- . port services, for example. One might cite the Canadian Pacific Steamships on the Atlantic and the Pacific, and Canadian cargo vessels ply the waters of the Atlantic on a competitive basis. While they may be registered in London, nevertheless the bottoms are Canadian.
As a small country we have built up great services. Our Canadian banks, our international banking system, which astounds many of the Americans, has branches all over the world. The same is true of Canadian insurance. One of the amazing things about Canadian insurance companies is the amount of business they do in the orient. These are peculiar things about our Canadian economy, and in order to maintain this very high level 
of international trade, we need some kind of control of currency, or some kind of international stabilizing agreement; otherwise we shall suffer in Canada far more than any other nation in the world.
We have been singularly blessed in that we have given to our workers a great amount- of power. The Canadian workman has at his hands many more horse-power than virtually the worker of any other country. Productivity per man is high, and we have been able to produce per man-hour a very large quantity of goods.	-
The great problem with us in Canada now, as it will be for some time, is how to balance our imports with our exports. By reason of our peculiar position we are far more of an exporting country than an importing. We export many times the quantity of goods that a country of slightly over twelve millions could ever expect, under present conditions, to consume at home. That is, of course, a problem of population.
I should now like briefly to mention one or two of the clauses in the Bretton Woods agreement. I am not on the banking and commerce committee, so that this will be my only chance to discuss this vital matter. In the preamble six basic purposes are set out. I will quote only the first sentence of each:
(i)	To promote international monetary cooperation.
(ii)	To facilitate the expansion and balanced growth of international trade.
(iii)	To promote exchange stability and maintain orderly exchange arrangements.
(iv)	To assist in the establishment of a multilateral system of payments in respect of current transactions between members and in the elimination of foreign exchange restrictions which hamper the growth of world trade.
(v)	To give confidence to members by making the fund's resources available to them under adequate safeguards . . .
(vi)	In accordance with the above, to shorten the duration and lessen the degree of disequilibrium in the international balances of payments of members.
Nothing could be more praiseworthy than these objects, and in the final clause of the agreements in annex C, under the heading, "the international monetary fund", it is stated:
Since foreign trade affects the standard of life of every people, all countries have a vital interest in the system of exchange of national currencies and the regulations and conditions which govern its working. Because these monetary transactions are international exchanges, the nations must agree on the basic rules which govern the exchanges if the system is to work smoothly. When they do no-t agree, and when single nations and small groups of nations attempt by special and different regulations of the foreign exchanges to gain trade advantages, the result is instability, a reduced volume of

Bretton Woods Agreements
foreign trade, and damage to national economies. This course of action is likely to lead to economic warfare and to endanger the world's peace.
Those are the basic purposes of the agreement, and surely no one will quarrel with them.
Fault has been found with the method of establishing currencies on a gold basis or on. a basis attached to gold. Well, what does the agreement say with regard to par values of currency? Article IV states:
The par value of the currency of each member shall he expressed in terms of gold as a common denominator or in terms of the United States dollar of the weight .and fineness in effect on July 1, 1944.
That is merely another way of saying "gold". Then it says that all computations relating to currencies shall be on the basis of their par value. It states that foreign exchange dealings shall be based on parity.- section 3-and that gold purchases shall be based on par value. Then section 4, article IV deals with obligations regarding exchange stability. Each member undertakes to collaborate with the fund to promote exchange stability. Each member undertakes, through appropriate measures consistent with the agreement, to promote within its territories exchange transactions between its currency and the currencies of other members. All these are basic fundamental rules of international trade.
There is, however, the method by which the parity of exchanges shall be fixed, and that appears in article 20, section 4. It merely states that each country shall settle its own parity of its own exchange. That is to me, Mr. Speaker, the crux of the whole question- the method of arriving at parity or of arriving? at the currency exchange value in gold of the various members of the agreement. At the present time the huge majority of currencies have a fictitiously high value in. terms of the United States dollar, in terms of gold and in terms of the Canadian dollar. I believe the franc is valued at two cents; but its actual purchasing power, according to the soldiers who have come back, is about one-eighth of a cent,. The lira and all the other European currencies have been given, I think unwisely, a fictitiously high value.
Before we can arrive at some degree of currency stabilization, there must be a period during which the currencies will be allowed tc. find their own value in terms of gold. I do not believe this can be done quickly; in fact it is a comparatively long-term operation; but before the agreement can become operative that has to be done, and it will be an extremely
difficult matter to arrive at. To me that is the great difficulty in the whole working out of the Bretton Woods agreement.
When the last workable gold parity was arrived at by the Herschell committee in the seventies of the last century there was a free gold market. That free gold market had been working for twenty or twenty-five years. They tied the pound and the dollar to gold at the then level of eighty-four shillings and sixpence, which had been the approximate mean value for some years past. That became known as the gold standard and brought tremendous prosperity to the countries which adopted the gold standard at that time. I think they were Great Britain, the United States, Germany and France. I do not know whether Italy came in or not; I think she did later, to a degree. But the gold countries virtually ruined or did not allow the great expansion they enjoyed because of their expanded international trade to the, rest of the world which lived on the silver standard, namely, the continents of Asia, Africa, India and certain parts of South America. There was not the tremendous industrial expansion; there was not the great trade boom in the silver countries that there was in the gold countries. Silver was manipulated, changed in value, and many times there were great crises in China and in India because of the manipulation and variation in prices of silver as compared with gold.
I do not propose at this time to talk about bimetalism, but I wish to say this, that while the monetary conference at Bretton Woods put in one paragraph concerning bimetalism, serious consideration must be given to providing the rest of the world with stable currencies convertible into the hard currency which will eventually be arrived at under this agreement. It is going to take many years, but it must be considered on this Norths American continent, particularly by Canada, which is a large gold and silver producing country and also a country which trades to a large extent with the silver standard countries of the world, Asia and China.
We in Canada are dependent upon a stable exchange. Probably we are more dependent upon stable rates of exchange than any other country in the world at the present time. We are in the focal point, situated between the sterling bloc, the gold exchange currency of the United States, and,, by geography at any rate, the closed economy of Russia. If we as a small country cannot come to some arrangement by which our currency and our trade is not at the behest of the great trading nations
Bretton Woods Agreements

which can control managed currencies, and which, because of their great wealth, can jockey with international currencies to our disadvantage; if we as a long-term exporting country cannot be sure that we trade in a currency which is convertible, stable and exchangeable, our future is extremely dark. Therefore I say that the Bretton Woods conference and the working out of the Bretton Woods proposals probably mean more to us than to any other country in the world. If we cannot get stable exchange; if we cannot provide our industries and primary producers with a medium by which they can make' long-term contracts, then we are going to live from hand to mouth, be at the beck and call of managed currencies, return to international banditry, and as a great producer of primary products and capital goods we shall suffer more than any other country I can think of.

Mr. Speaker, in the present debate on the Bretton Woods agreement I do not hope to be able to add a great deal more to the arguments which have been advanced by my colleagues, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). I regard their arguments as indisputable, and I believe that we have a tight to expect, before this debate closes, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) will attempt to answer the arguments of both these hon. members. If he does not then he is not doing justice to the people of this country.
Leading off in the debate the Minister of Finance gave an excellent speech. He certainly did impress the house with the immense importance of this Bretton Woods agreement. I cap only state that if the Bretton Woods agreement is as important as he led us to believe it to be-and I am inclined to agree with him-then, he owes it to the people of this country to permit this house to go to any length, leaving no stone unturned, in the most thorough investigation of everything involved in this agreement. I said the other day in another debate I was convinced that_ the present financial system, which is international and knows no boundaries, was on its last legs. There is no question but that prior to the war circumstances proved that the present international financial system was a failure in this modern age of scientific production. I have no doubt that as a result of the breakdown of this system the war was brought on. I am not satisfied that the root cause of war i3 simply a lust for power on the part of some individual, just arising at the moment. The reasons for war are deep-rooted. War has a background; there is a cause for it, and, as

the hon. member for Lethbridge adequately expressed it this .afternoon, the cause lies in the economic field.
In saying that the present financial system is on its last legs, that it has perhaps destroyed itself, I am reminded of a snake attempting to eat its own tail until it eats itself all away, if that could be possible. That is the way the present financial system seems to have worked. But those in charge of high finance say, "No; we must save this system. We must bring about something or other that will force it to work." I believe an attempt is being made throughout the world to force what I regard as an obsolete financial system to work. My logic, which I do not think is faulty, would lead me to believe that if we are to force the present financial system to work, then we must force people to obey its dictates; and as , we do so, we take from the peoples of the world their right to freedom. There is no question about that. I am perfectly convinced that the various world moves that are being made, dovetailing as they seem to do into each other are an attempt to set up a dictator-., ship which will be nothing more or less than a glorified world state. Speaking from the economic viewpoint, I regard the Bretton Woods agreement as part of the machinery to bring into being that glorified world slave state.
May I now make another and slightly different observation. I have always regarded the British empire as a bulwark of Christian democracy. Some people ridicule that statement. I am not concerned about their ridicule; a conviction is a conviction. As one lives, as one thinks, as one reads and studies, one forms certain convictions. One conviction I have formed is that the British empire is a bulwark of Christian democracy, which means freedom of the people. There is no doubt in my mind that there are forces abroad , in the world to-day-I do not know how one could personify them-which may be involved in systems or movements, things like this measure, which are brought into existence for the purpose of destroying the British empire; for as long as the British peoples stand for justice and freedom and the kind of Christian democracy I visualize, then there cannot be a world slave state.
At the present time I do not despair of the situation, but there is. no doubt that Great Britain is in most terribly straitened circumstances. She had the fortitude to suffer and come through the war on top. She has been pounded almost to death. If the same thing had happened to some other nations I am sure they would have gone under long ago. The industries of Great Britain have

Bretton Woods Agreements
been almost destroyed, and it will be a long time before #they are rebuilt. Her production is low; the capital equipment of her factories has been largely destroyed. Although in the early days of the war she stood alone, she has emerged as one of the victorious nations. Yet to-day as far as Europe is concerned Great Britain is in danger of becoming a second, third or fourth-rate power. That is one danger. The other danger is that under such measures as we have before us to-night she may become a second, third or fourth-rate economic power in the world. If that be so, I ask: can the Canadian people, as part of that commonwealth of nations, think for one moment of aiding and abetting the destruction of that empire? I do not see how we can. I say to the minister that he should do everything in his power to give this agreement the closest scrutiny and to give this parliament an opportunity to investigate it thoroughly. After all, I think the experts are doing work upon it and have been for some time. Parliaments come and parliaments go, but the experts seem to remain forever. Finance ministers come and finance ministers go, but their deputies and their experts behind the scenes seem to remain forever.
It is all very well for the minister to place upon the doorstep of parliament at this late hour a measure such as this and say, "Well, the experts have gone through it, and my advisers have advised me that everything is all right." But, remember, it is parliament that has to act and to say whether or not Canada is to subscribe to the agreement. The experts are absolved from that responsibility. Since we are talking about experts and about responsible government, it surprises me that the present government is so anxious to do things on an international or a world scale, when I do not believe the minister can point to one thing the government has solved successfully on a national scale.
We did a magnificent job during the war; I know all about that. The minister is quite likely to say, "See what Canada did in the matter of finance during the war." Well, what happened was this: A war breaks out, and the green light is given to the financial institutions to expand their credit. And of course, when there is an expansion of credit through a process of debt, you can do almost anything.
It is true we 'have done a magnificent job and, we might say, in a way, a magnificent job financially. But our problem is not solved, because the minister has done that job by plunging the nation into irreparable debt. Personally I hold no hope whatsoever that
the national debt of Canada will be ultimately paid. I do not wish to be misunderstood. I do not say that Canadians who hold war bonds will not be paid. Of course those bonds will be retired through some sort of process of refunding; eventually the banking institutions of this country will hold the debt, and the people of Canada will pay toll for the rest of Canada's existence. That is my personal opinion.
I say that I do not see one national problem in the financial field the government has ever solved. One hon. member whispers to me: Look at old age pensions. Well, that is a financial problem. Is it solved? One could go on and on naming them. Yet the government seems so anxious to launch out into some great international scheme, apparently supposing that by making the problem larger they can solve it more easily.
Well, one does not wipe out crime by joining together two penitentiaries. One must get at the root of the problem, and tackle it at home first. Make a success of it at home, and then the government will be able to say, "We are now qualified to tackle things on an international scale."
As I said a minute ago, I urged the minister to make way for the house to give every possible consideration to every possible detail of the measure. I am suggesting that he should send it to the banking and commerce committee. I do not know if that is his intention.

When at the last session of parliament we were discussing the San Francisco conference- not the charter-I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a number of questions. Bretton TFoods Agreements

At page 309 of Hansard for March 28, 1945, the Prime Minister, answering certain questions I had asked him, said:
I think I have come to the end of what I have found it necessary to say this afternoon in answer to questions raised in this debate; but I recall that my hon. friends of the Social Credit group also directed a number of questions to me. Last evening the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) asked a number of questions and requested that I reply to them to-day.
Then the Prime Minister made certain answers, for which we thank him. Here are some of the questions and answers:
If the proposals are adopted, would the control of this nation's currency and credit remain within our own power? In other words, would we retain absolute control over-our own currency and credit?
The Prime Minister answered as follows:
I might say that before my hon. friend asked that question, I had prepared an answer to give to his leader in relation to what he had had to say on the Bretton Woods proposals, and I will give this answer to both hon. members and to their party at this time.
A word as to the speeches made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). The contribution of these hon. members to the debate consisted very largely of an attack on the resolutions of the united nations monetary and financial conference, generally known as the Bretton Woods proposals. I confess that I am somewhat surprised to find the Social Credit party bringing aid and comfort to the more reactionary international bankers who have been the chief critics of the Bretton Woods proposals.
' I might say that the hon. member for Lethbridge answered that later on. Then the Prime Minister continued:
The hon. member for Acadia asked: Does approval of section 3 of the resolution before the house imply an endorsement of the final act of the Bretton Woods agreement? The short answer to that question is, no-
Of course it refers to the San Francisco conference.
-the house is not in this resolution being asked to endorse the Bretton Woods proposals. At the same time, I am convinced that collaboration among nations in the economic and financial field is a vital part of any effective system of international security.
He does not say that we are being asked to endorse Bretton Woods; but he certainly says, by inference at least, that he is in favour of the proposals. I shall not take the time to Tead the whole column, but later on-I am not taking it out of its text-he goes on to say:
We should be making a very poor approach indeed to the great problems to be dealt with at San Francisco, if we failed to 'take a constructive attitude toward the proposals which the
[Mr. Hansell.l
delegates of forty-four united nations assembled at Bretton Woods have, after long study and deliberation, put forward for the consideration of governments.
The next question is:
Do any of the proposals and principles involve the return to the gold standard?
I know that technically the Prime Minister is talking about San Francisco, but the two have become so linked together that I do not see how you can separate the one from the other. At least this is what the Prime Minister said:
The answer to that question is, no.
Then a little later on in the same page:
Mr. Mackenzie King:	The next question is:
If so, will the government, as far as it is concerned, oppose such a step?
What did the Prime Minister say? Here are his words:
So far as I am concerned that is answered by
the previous reply.
So that he was going to oppose any step if it meant a return to the gold standard. I think the hon. member for Lethbridge and the hon. member for' Acadia have to my satisfaction, and I think to the satisfaction of anyone who will look into their arguments, made out a case for these agreements meaning an absolute return, to the gold standard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: What does my hon. friend mean by the gold standard?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: I know the minister will try to get me on some technical point.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: We will say, whatever ii means.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Whatever it means, I do not care.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: We do not want gold at all.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
It is in the agreement, as was noted by the hon. member for Acadia. I think it will stand repeating. Article IV on page 20 which is headed "Par values of currencies", reads:
Section 1. Expression of par values.
(a) The par value of the currency of each member shall be expressed in terms of gold as a common denominator or in terms of the United States dollar of the weight and fineness in effect on July 1, 1944.
If it is not a return to the gold standard, why is that clause in there? The minister may ask me a technical question, but let him answer that question when we are in committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I certainly will.

Bretton Woods Agreements .

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I should like to quote now from a man who should know. The minister questioned one authority who was quoted to-night, but I should like to quote Paul Einzig. I think he is well known as one of the experts, and in an article which appeared in the Daily Express of August 10, 1944, entitled, "A plain man's guide to the menace of Bretton Woods"-evidently he regarded Bretton Woods as a menace

he made this statement:
It must be clear to those who understand the meaning of the report of the Bretton Woods international monetary conference, published in a white -paper before the bank holiday, that the experts of forty-four nations have agreed on -a return to the gold standard -after the w-ar.
The minister had better ask Professor Einzig what he means by the gold standard. He goes on to say:
Unfortunately, very few laymen can possibly understand the report. If the public were to realize what it is being led into it would raise its voice in a powerful protest, instead of allowing -the experts a free hand to do their worst, as they did in 1925.
Perhaps I had better say who Paul Einzig is. He is a doctor of science in political economy. He was, educated at Brasov, the oriental academy of Budapest and the university of Paris. He was Paris correspondent of the Financial News in 1921; foreign editor in 1923; political correspondent in 1939. He became a British subject by naturalization in 1929. His publications are: "Le Mouvement des Prix," 1923; "International Gold Movement," 1929; "The Bank for International Settlements," 1930; "The Fight for Financial Supremacy," 1931. I will not read all the dates. He wrote the "World Economic Crisis", "Behind the Scenes of International Finance," "The Tragedy of the Pound", "Finance and Politics", "Finance and Politics a year later", "Montagu Norman", "The Comedy of the Pound," "The Economic Foundations of Fascism," "The Sterling-Dollar-Franc Tangle", "Germany's Default", "France's Crisis," "The Future of Gold," "World Finance since 1941", "Bankers, Statesmen and Economists", "Exchange Clearing", "Monetary Reform in Theory and Practice," "The Theory of Forward Exchange". I am just half through. Is the minister satisfied?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: I did not think my hon. friend liked experts.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: It takes an expert to catch an expert.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
We have to pit one expert against another. His recreations are given, but I do not think we need go into that. It is stated fhat this gentleman likes music, reading and walking. He certainly has gone places anyway. In -the same article he makes this strong statement:
In 1925 the gold standard was, at any rate, restored in the full light of publicity. The public knew what was happening. It had only itself to blame for having failed -to heed the advice of the lone voice crying in the wilderness

that of the Daily Express prominently among them-warning the country against the consequences of the proposed step.
In 1944, on the other hand, the -public is only too well aware that a -return to_ the gold standard would, be unmitigated evil, spelling ruin and misery. It would now be politically impossible to reintroduce the gold standard openly.
But it is being introduced just the same, this time in disguise, under another name.
The public is lulled into a false feeling of security by being told again and again that the new system is not the gold standard.
And again:
Yet once the plan is translated into intelligible English and is denuded^ of all _ camouflage, every layman of normal intelligence is bound to realize that it is the gold standard, the full gold standard, and nothing but the gold standard.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Explain that away, now.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is nearly eleven o'clock, and the next part of what I had to say would lose its continuity, if I stopped at that hour, but I once again urge the minister to help us. We are not here merely to put over some particular theory; all of us, I am sure, are interested in the preservation of our people and in the maintenance of real democracy in the world-; and if it is probable, as Paul Einzig and others say it is, that this document is dangerous, let t!*e minister not. be a victim any more than the rest of us; let us in the banking and commerce committee give the act the full light of day. I would- ask him to consent to call the greatest experts. Let us call, if need be, Mr. Morgenthau, who was one of the United States representatives. I refer to him because he is near at hand; I do- not expect they are going to send to Norway, or the Netherlands, or some other remote place. But let. them call Lord Keynes.
One other thing I wish to say in the minute or two I have left. Is it not surprising, since the minister has told us of the tremendous importance of this document, that he has left it until now, December 6, to bring it before parliament, when it should be signed before the end of the year, and the deadline for the closing of parliament is supposed to be December 15^ I do not want to impute motives, but does it not seem strange that this act was printed by the Printer to the King's Most Excellent Majesty in 1944 f yet
War Finance Committee

the matter has not been open for discussion; it was not sent to the banking and commerce committee, which in the spring of this year did not have anything to do, and now, at this late hour, such an important document as the minister himself claims' it to be is left on our doorstep. That proceeding should be resented by every member of this house, and the committee should call the greatest experts, no matter where they have to be brought from.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Experts on both sides, too.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND-INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Yes, let us have the facts and nothing but the facts. I urge the minister so to do.
